These are the two directions of the PCA arrows, and the stretch factors are the factor variances \(\delta_1^2\) and \(\delta_2^2\). The next subsection shows that this is no coincidence. 4.4.2 Why the PCA directions are eigenvectors Start from the covariance matrix and the PCA split of Section 4.2, \(A=\Gamma\Delta\) with \(\Gamma\) a rotation and \(\Delta\) diagonal: \[ S=AA'=(\Gamma\Delta)(\Gamma\Delta)'=\Gamma\Delta\Delta'\Gamma'=\Gamma\Delta^2\Gamma' , \] using \((\Gamma\Delta)'=\Delta'\Gamma'\) and \(\Delta'=\Delta\) for a diagonal matrix. Now multiply both sides by \(\Gamma\) on the right. Because \(\Gamma'\Gamma=I\), the last two matrices cancel: \[ S\Gamma=\Gamma\Delta^2\Gamma'\Gamma=\Gamma\Delta^2 . \] Read this column by column. Column \(l\) of \(S\Gamma\) is \(S\gamma_l\). Column \(l\) of \(\Gamma\Delta^2\) is \(\delta_l^2\gamma_l\), because multiplying by a diagonal matrix on the right just scales each column. So \[ S\gamma_l=\delta_l^2\,\gamma_l , \] which is exactly the eigenvector equation: each PCA direction \(\gamma_l\) is an eigenvector of \(S\), and its eigenvalue is \(\delta_l^2\), the variance of factor \(l\). In the figure, the points on the blue line are stretched by \(\delta_1^2\) and those on the red line by \(\delta_2^2\). And because PCA makes the first arrow as long as possible, the first component is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, the second the one with the next largest, and so on. The connection also runs the other way, and that is how PCA is computed in practice. A matrix whose eigenvectors span the space can be written as \[ S=VKV^{-1}, \] with the eigenvectors as the columns of \(V\) and the eigenvalues in the diagonal matrix \(K=\operatorname{diag}(\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_p)\) (\(K\) is a capital kappa), read from right to left: \(V^{-1}\) changes to the coordinates of the eigenvectors, \(K\) stretches each axis, and \(V\) changes back (3Blue1Brown, chapters 13 and 14). This is the eigendecomposition. For a general matrix, \(V\) is not a rotation and \(V^{-1}\) has to be computed. Covariance matrices are special: they are symmetric, \(S'=S\), and for a symmetric matrix the eigenvectors can always be chosen perpendicular and of length one (the spectral theorem). Then \(V\) is a rotation, \(V^{-1}=V'\), and \[ S=VKV' \] has exactly the form of the PCA split \(S=\Gamma\Delta^2\Gamma'\): \(\Gamma=V\) and \(\Delta^2=K\), up to the order and signs of the columns. The eigenvalues of a covariance matrix are variances, so they are never negative. One call to eigen() therefore replaces the slider: S <- cov(cola) e <- eigen(S) e$values # eigenvalues: the factor variances delta_l^2 ## [1] 2.00131488 0.09868512 e$vectors # eigenvectors: the directions gamma_l (columns), up to sign ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.6882736 -0.7254512 ## [2,] 0.7254512 0.6882736 A <- e$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(e$values)) # the PCA choice of A = Gamma Delta A %*% t(A) # reproduces S ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 1.00 0.95 ## [2,] 0.95 1.10 The \(l\)-th principal component is the eigenvector \(\gamma_l\) of \(S\) with the \(l\)-th largest eigenvalue, and the variance of its scores is that eigenvalue, \(\delta_l^2\). What Sections 4.1 and 4.2 showed about the factor variances now reads as a statement about eigenvalues: they add up to the total variance, \(\delta_1^2+\dots+\delta_p^2=\operatorname{tr}(S)\), so component \(l\) carries the share \(\delta_l^2/\operatorname{tr}(S)\) of it. For Coke and Pepsi the market component carries 95%. PCA of the covariance matrix finds the variable with the most units, not the most interesting direction. The right panel shows the remedy: standardise each variable first, \(z_{tj}=(x_{tj}-\bar x_j)/s_j\). Standardised values do not depend on the units, so neither do their components. The covariance matrix of standardised variables is the correlation matrix \(R\); for two variables its components are always the sum and the difference, \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)'\) and \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)'\) (Section 4.4). PCA is not scale-invariant: changing the units of a variable changes the components, not just their units (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.4). When the variables are measured in different units, use PCA of the correlation matrix. Every variable then has variance one, \(\operatorname{tr}(R)=p\), and each starts with an equal claim on the components. Working with \(S\) is appropriate when all variables share a unit and their variances are comparable (sales of two brands in the same units, test scores on the same scale). 4.5.2 More variables: the states With more variables and very different units, the effect is extreme. There is no single correct number; Everitt and Hothorn (Section 3.8) list the common rules of thumb: Percentage of variance. Keep the components before the flat part. For the states, 70% asks for 2 components and 90% for 4; the Kaiser rule keeps 1 (the second eigenvalue, 0.99, misses the cut-off by a hair), Jolliffe’s 0.7 keeps 3, and the elbow at component 2 says one. These are guides, not tests: choose with the purpose in mind. Two components are needed for a scatterplot; an index needs one; an input to a later analysis may need more. Check your understanding In a scree plot, the elbow marks the component with the largest eigenvalue where the eigenvalues stop falling steeply and level off the component that explains exactly 50% where the eigenvalues become negative For a correlation matrix, the Kaiser rule keeps components with eigenvalue above 1 because 1 is the variance of each standardised variable, so such components explain more than one variable eigenvalues above 1 are statistically significant the total variance is 1 components with \(\delta_l^2<1\) are negatively correlated Answers 1 b. 2 a. 4.7 Reconstruction and unusual observations With \(p\) variables, keeping only a few components loses information. How much, and for which observations? Because \(\Gamma\) is a rotation, the scores can be turned back into the data: \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma \mathbf f_t =\sum_{l=1}^p f_{tl}\gamma_l\). Keeping only the first \(k\) terms gives the best approximation from \(k\) numbers, \[ \hat{\mathbf x}_t=\sum_{l=1}^k f_{tl}\gamma_l , \] and the sum of the squared errors over all observations and variables is \((n-1)(\delta_{k+1}^2+\dots+\delta_p^2)\): the variance of the dropped components. The covariance matrix is approximated in the same way, \(S\approx A_kA_k'\) with the first \(k\) columns of \(A\) (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.7). fig_reconstruct <- function(states = c("Alaska", "Hawaii", "Texas")) { Z <- scale(X6); G <- st_cor$rotation; Y <- st_cor$x rec <- function(s, k) drop(G[, 1:k, drop = FALSE] %*% Y[s, 1:k]) # x-hat = sum of the first k score * weight d <- purrr::map_dfr(states, function(s) bind_rows( tibble(state = s, var = colnames(X6), m = "actual", z = Z[s, ]), purrr::map_dfr(1:3, function(k) tibble(state = s, var = colnames(X6), z = rec(s, k), m = paste0("k = ", k))))) |> mutate(var = factor(var, levels = colnames(X6)), state = factor(state, levels = states)) ggplot(d, aes(var, z)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_col(data = filter(d, m == "actual"), fill = "grey80", width = 0.7) + geom_point(data = filter(d, m != "actual"), aes(colour = m, shape = m), size = 2.6, position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("k = 1" = col_a1, "k = 2" = "#7b4fb5", "k = 3" = col_a2), name = "reconstruction") + scale_shape_manual(values = c("k = 1" = 16, "k = 2" = 17, "k = 3" = 15), name = "reconstruction") + facet_wrap(~ state, ncol = 3) + labs(x = NULL, y = "standardised value (bars: actual)") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1), legend.position = "top") } # draw the figure fig_reconstruct() Texas follows the common pattern: one component (blue) already gets the signs and rough sizes of all six standardised values. Alaska and Hawaii do not: one component misses them badly, and only two or three components come close. Recall from Section 2.6 that these are the states with unusual combinations. This is no coincidence: the squared Mahalanobis distance is the sum of the standardised squared scores, \[ d_t^2=\mathbf x_t'S^{-1}\mathbf x_t=\sum_{l=1}^p\frac{f_{tl}^2}{\delta_l^2}=\sum_{l=1}^p\varepsilon_{tl}^2, \] because \(S^{-1}=\Gamma\Delta^{-2}\Gamma'\). A large score on a small component, a direction in which the cloud is thin, counts heavily. Unusual states are exactly those that the first components describe badly. Z <- scale(X) for (k in 1:4) { Zhat <- pc$x[, 1:k, drop = FALSE] %*% t(pc$rotation[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]) # reconstruction from k scores cat(k, "components: squared error", round(sum((Z - Zhat)^2), 1), "= (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues", round(49 * sum(pc$sdev[-(1:k)]^2), 1), "\n") } ## 1 components: squared error 119.8 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 119.8 ## 2 components: squared error 71.4 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 71.4 ## 3 components: squared error 32.7 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 32.7 ## 4 components: squared error 17 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 17 Check your understanding Reconstructing standardised data from the first \(k\) components leaves a squared error equal to zero \((n-1)\) times the sum of the dropped eigenvalues \((n-1)\) times the sum of the kept eigenvalues the largest eigenvalue A state with a large score on the last component is typical is unusual in a direction where the cloud is thin, so it has a large Mahalanobis distance has a large value on every variable has been reconstructed exactly by the first component Answers 1 b. 2 b. 4.8 What PCA is, and what it is not 4.8.1 One choice of structural form PCA is one answer to the identification problem of the Introduction: of all the matrices \(A\) with \(AA'=S\), it picks the one whose first column is longest. That is a choice made for convenience (order the directions by variance), not one forced by the data. For the flights, where we know the true shocks from the manual, the first principal component explains 91% of the variance, but it is neither the headwind nor the load: it is a mixture of both. cloud_pts <- function(X, alpha = 0.45) geom_point(data = tibble(x = X[, 1], y = X[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = alpha, size = 1.5) fig_pca_vs_truth <- function() { S <- cov(air_X); e <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE) G <- e$vectors; if (G[1, 1] < 0) G[, 1] <- -G[, 1]; if (det(G) < 0) G[, 2] <- -G[, 2] A_pca <- G %*% diag(sqrt(e$values)) el <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(S), 1); el <- tibble(x = el[1, ], y = el[2, ]) panel <- function(M, labs, title) { lab <- tibble(x = M[1, ] * (1 + 0.9 / sqrt(colSums(M^2))), y = M[2, ] * (1 + 0.9 / sqrt(colSums(M^2))), txt = labs, col = c(col_a1, col_a2)) ggplot() + axes0 + cloud_pts(air_X, 0.25) + geom_path(data = el, aes(x, y), linewidth = 0.9) + geom_segment(data = tibble(xend = M[1, ], yend = M[2, ], col = c(col_a1, col_a2)), aes(0, 0, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.5, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed")) + geom_label(data = lab, aes(x, y, label = txt, colour = I(col)), size = 4, fontface = "bold", label.size = 0, fill = alpha("white", 0.8), lineheight = 0.9) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.2, 4.2), ylim = c(-4.2, 4.2)) + labs(title = title, x = "flight time (min)", y = "fuel (100 kg)") } panel(A_pca, c("PC1", "PC2"), "PCA: longest first column") + panel(air_A, c("headwind", "load"), "The true shocks (from the manual)") } # draw the figure fig_pca_vs_truth() So it is tempting, but risky, to give components names such as “all-round ability” or “quality of life”. Everitt and Hothorn quote Marriott (1974): “no mathematical method is, or could be, designed to give physically meaningful results.” A component that has an obvious meaning reflects a strongly structured data set, or luck. PCA is safest as a tool for description and compression: a low-dimensional map of the data, an index, or fewer inputs for a later analysis. 4.8.2 Practical points Correlation is needed. PCA can only compress correlated variables. If the variables are uncorrelated and standardised, every eigenvalue is one and no component is better than any other. Scale. Results depend on the units unless the variables are standardised (Section 4.5). Outliers. One observation can change the correlations, and hence the components (the PNG athlete). Look at the data first, as in Chapter 2. Signs and order. Signs are arbitrary. Components with nearly equal eigenvalues are unstable: a slightly different sample can swap them or mix them. Sample size. Larger samples give more stable components, especially when eigenvalues are close together. Rules such as \(n>100\) or \(n>5p\) have little evidence behind them (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.12). Regression on components. Highly correlated explanatory variables can be replaced by their first few components (principal components regression). The components with the largest variance need not be the ones that best predict the outcome, however: Everitt and Hothorn’s air-pollution example finds low-variance components that matter (Section 3.10.3). Check your understanding For the flights, the first principal component is exactly the headwind shock is exactly the load shock is a mixture of both: PCA picks a convenient rotation, not the true one does not exist because the shocks are independent Six uncorrelated standardised variables give a correlation-matrix PCA in which the first component explains everything every eigenvalue is 1, so there is nothing to compress the components are the variables in order of their means the scree plot has a sharp elbow Answers 1 c. 2 b. 4.9 Two sets of variables: canonical correlation PCA looks at the relations within one set of variables. Sometimes the question is about the relation between two sets: aptitude tests and achievement tests, plant growth and weather, or, for the states, education (illiteracy, high-school graduation) and health and safety (life expectancy, murder). Many pairwise correlations between the sets are hard to summarise, and the correlations within each set get in the way. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA, Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.13) replaces each set by a few linear combinations. Collect the first set in the vector \(\mathbf x_t\) (\(p_1\) variables) and the second in \(\mathbf y_t\) (\(p_2\) variables). CCA finds weights \(w^{(x)}\) and \(w^{(y)}\) such that the two linear combinations \(w^{(x)\prime}\mathbf x_t\) and \(w^{(y)\prime}\mathbf y_t\), the canonical variates, have the largest possible correlation \(r_1\), the first canonical correlation. Then it finds a second pair of combinations with the largest correlation \(r_2\) among combinations uncorrelated with the first pair, and so on, up to \(\min(p_1,p_2)\) pairs. Like the principal components, the weights are eigenvectors: with \(R_{xx}\) and \(R_{yy}\) the correlation matrices within the two sets and \(R_{xy}=R_{yx}'\) the correlations between them, the weights \(w^{(x)}\) are the eigenvectors of \(R_{xx}^{-1}R_{xy}R_{yy}^{-1}R_{yx}\), the weights \(w^{(y)}\) those of \(R_{yy}^{-1}R_{yx}R_{xx}^{-1}R_{xy}\), and the eigenvalues are the squared canonical correlations \(r_l^2\). For the states, the first canonical correlation is 0.71. In standardised variables, the first pair is approximately \[ \text{education index }1\propto-0.98\,\text{Illiteracy}+0.19\,\text{HSGrad},\qquad \text{health index }1\propto0.30\,\text{LifeExp}-0.95\,\text{Murder}: \] low illiteracy goes with low murder rates. The second canonical correlation, 0.37, is much weaker. Its pair puts positive weight on both variables of each set, \[ \text{education index }2\propto0.60\,\text{Illiteracy}+0.80\,\text{HSGrad},\qquad \text{health index }2\propto0.75\,\text{LifeExp}+0.66\,\text{Murder}: \] what is left once the first pair is accounted for: a weak tendency for states with both more illiteracy and more high-school graduates to have both longer lives and more murders. With two variables per set, the second education index is the only one left that is uncorrelated with the first, so it plays the role of a residual: not a regression residual, but the direction in the education variables that the first index leaves out. The same holds for the second health and safety index. fig_cca <- function() { U <- Zst[, c("Illiteracy", "HSGrad")] %*% cc_states$xcoef V <- Zst[, c("LifeExp", "Murder")] %*% cc_states$ycoef U <- U * sqrt(nrow(U) - 1); V <- V * sqrt(nrow(V) - 1) # canonical variates with variance 1 s1 <- sign(cc_states$xcoef["HSGrad", 1]) # first pair: high = more educated s2 <- sign(cc_states$xcoef["HSGrad", 2]) # second pair: positive weights d <- tibble(abb = state.abb, u1 = s1 * U[, 1], v1 = s1 * V[, 1], u2 = s2 * U[, 2], v2 = s2 * V[, 2]) p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(u1, v1)) + geom_point(colour = col_a1, size = 2) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = abb), size = 2.8, colour = "grey35", seed = 5, max.overlaps = 15) + labs(title = sprintf("First pair: correlation %.2f", cc_states$cor[1]), x = "education index 1", y = "health and safety index 1") p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(u2, v2)) + geom_point(colour = col_a2, size = 2) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = abb), size = 2.8, colour = "grey35", seed = 5, max.overlaps = 15) + labs(title = sprintf("Second pair: correlation %.2f", cc_states$cor[2]), x = "education index 2", y = "health and safety index 2") p1 + p2 } # draw the figure fig_cca() Most states lie close to the line in the left panel. Nevada stands out at the bottom right: well educated, but with a high murder rate. Zs <- scale(X) cc <- cancor(Zs[, c("Illiteracy", "HS Grad")], Zs[, c("Life Exp", "Murder")]) cc$cor # canonical correlations ## [1] 0.7102436 0.3651655 R <- cor(X[, c("Illiteracy", "HS Grad", "Life Exp", "Murder")]) Rxx <- R[1:2, 1:2]; Rxy <- R[1:2, 3:4]; Ryy <- R[3:4, 3:4] sqrt(eigen(solve(Rxx) %*% Rxy %*% solve(Ryy) %*% t(Rxy))$values) # the same, from the eigenvalues ## [1] 0.7102436 0.3651655 CCA is used less than the other methods in this course because its variates are often hard to interpret (Everitt and Hothorn’s examples, head sizes of brothers and depression in Los Angeles, show both a clear and a less clear case). It is the natural generalisation of the multiple correlation of regression to several outcomes. Check your understanding Canonical correlation analysis finds the directions of largest variance in one set of variables linear combinations of two sets of variables that are as highly correlated as possible clusters of observations the regression of each variable on all others With 2 variables in one set and 4 in the other, the number of canonical correlations is 2 4 6 8 Answers 1 b. 2 a. 4.10 Summary Splitting \(A=C\Delta\) gives the shocks units: \(\Delta\) says how important each factor is, \(C\) how the variables combine them. The split needs a normalisation: ones on the diagonal (Cholesky, the regressor and the residual; symmetric root, each roommate’s own GPA), outside facts (structural), or columns of length one (PCA, so that the factor variances add up to the total variance). Every \(A\) with \(AA'=S\) fits the data; the squared length of each arrow (column) is the variance its shock carries. PCA turns the arrows until the first one is longest, then the second, and so on; the arrows come out perpendicular, so \(A=\Gamma\Delta\) is a stretch followed by a rotation. The scores \(\mathbf f_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t\) undo the rotation, the standardised scores undo the stretch too. Equivalently, the first principal component is the unit vector \(\gamma_1\) whose scores \(\gamma_1'\mathbf x_t\) have the largest variance; it is also the line closest to the cloud in the perpendicular sense. The components are the eigenvectors of \(S\), the directions that \(S\) only stretches, and their variances the eigenvalues \(\delta_l^2\). In the eigenbasis the covariance matrix is diagonal, \(\Gamma'S\Gamma=\Delta^2\): the scores are uncorrelated, and the eigenvalues add up to the total variance. PCA depends on the units: rescaling one variable swings the components towards it. With different units, use the correlation matrix (standardised variables). How many components is a judgement: share of variance, eigenvalues above average (Kaiser, Jolliffe), the scree plot. The biplot draws \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma\mathbf f_t\): scores as points, rows of \(\Gamma\) (the weights) as arrows; with standardised scores, the arrows are the rows of \(A=\Gamma\Delta\) (the loadings). Short arrows mark variables that the first two components represent poorly. The first \(k\) components give the best \(k\)-dimensional reconstruction; observations that it misses are the unusual combinations of Chapter 2. PCA is a convenient rotation, not a discovery of the true forces: use it to describe and compress, and label components with care. Canonical correlation extends the idea to two sets of variables. PCA keeps the directions in which the data vary most, and drops the rest. 4.10.1 Further reading Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 3 (principal components analysis, Sections 3.1 to 3.12; canonical correlation analysis, Section 3.13). 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra, chapters 9 (dot products and projections), 13 (change of basis) and 14 (eigenvectors and eigenvalues).

5 Multidimensional Scaling R code for this chapter: mds_figures.R (data and figures) and _common.R (shared helpers). Save both in one folder and run source("mds_figures.R"); every figure is then one function call, as shown under the Code buttons. Slides for this chapter: mds_slides.html (opens in a new tab; use the arrow keys to move between slides). So far every analysis started from a data matrix \(\mathbf X\): \(n\) observations, each measured on \(p\) variables. Some data arrive in a different form, as distances between the observations: travel times between places, how differently two members of Congress vote, how rarely two words are used together. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) turns such a table of distances into coordinates, a map. This chapter starts from the loop road of the Introduction, asks how much a table of distances reveals about the coordinates behind it, shows that MDS lands directly on the principal component scores of Chapter 4, connects the idea to the embeddings of modern AI, and then moves from straight-line distances to other kinds. Notation: \(d_{st}\) is the distance between observations \(s\) and \(t\), and the \(n\times n\) table of all of them is the distance matrix \(\mathbf D\). It is bold like the data matrix \(\mathbf X\) because it has one row for each observation, and so are the other matrices of this chapter with \(n\) rows. 5.1 Travel times on a loop road Picture again the town of the Introduction, whose eight places all sit on one loop road. For getting around, what matters is not the straight line between two places but the driving time along the road. At 30 km/h a full loop takes 41 minutes. MDS is given only the table of travel times between the places, and it looks for points in the plane whose straight-line distances reproduce the table as closely as possible. With no waiting, MDS finds a ring, with the places in driving order. Now a construction site between the Stadium and the Church makes everybody who drives through it wait. Drag the slider to add waiting time: the ring stretches open at the construction site, and once the wait passes 27.9 minutes nobody drives through the site any more, and MDS returns a line: one dimension is enough. (Classical MDS lays the line along its first dimension; Section 5.3 explains why.) The diagonal is zero, since getting from a place to itself takes no time, and the matrix is symmetric: the trip from the Church to the School takes as long as the trip back. Without waiting, each trip takes the shorter way around the loop. With the wait, the trips outlined in orange get longer: exactly those whose shortest way passes the site. A trip gets longer only until going around the other way is quicker; after that, the trip avoids the site. MDS never saw the map of the town, only such a distance matrix. Yet it recovered what matters for travel: the order of the places around the loop, and roughly how far apart they are in minutes. Only roughly, though: no map, in any number of dimensions, has travel times around a loop as its straight-line distances (Section 5.6.3 shows why). The ring is the best two-dimensional approximation that classical MDS finds, and without waiting its distances are 2.0 minutes off the travel times on average (the average distance error under the map). With a long wait, the travel times become distances along a line, and the line reproduces every one of them exactly. The rest of the chapter explains how this works, what MDS can and cannot recover, and where else the idea turns up. Every distance matrix has zeros on the diagonal (\(d_{tt}=0\)), is symmetric (\(d_{st}=d_{ts}\)), has no negative entries, and satisfies the triangle inequality, \(d_{su}\le d_{st}+d_{tu}\): a detour through \(t\) is never shorter. So the table holds \(n(n-1)/2\) distinct numbers, the entries above the diagonal. For an example with a known answer, take the 48 contiguous states (without Alaska and Hawaii), each represented by its centre (R’s state.center), and put the centres on a flat map in km, east and north of the middle of the country. On this map the distances are Euclidean. Here are five of them: us_D <- as.matrix(dist(us_X)) # all 48 x 48 distances between the state centres (km) round(us_D[c("WA", "CA", "TX", "FL", "ME"), c("WA", "CA", "TX", "FL", "ME")]) ## WA CA TX FL ME ## WA 0 1204 2529 3925 4374 ## CA 1204 0 1894 3415 4485 ## TX 2529 1894 0 1522 3009 ## FL 3925 3415 1522 0 2246 ## ME 4374 4485 3009 2246 0 5.2.2 Can we go back? In \(p\) dimensions a rotation has \(p(p-1)/2\) angles: one in two dimensions, three in three, six in four. It is the same count as the free angles of \(A\) in Section 3.7, where the shocks could be turned without changing \(\Sigma\). This is the same problem as in the Introduction. There, many matrices \(A\) gave the same covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), and they differed by a rotation of the shocks. Here, many maps give the same distance matrix \(\mathbf D\), and they differ by a rotation (or reflection) of the map. It takes a detour through inner products, which are easy to split into coordinates (Section 5.3.2). A small example shows what they are: three points on a map, \(\mathbf x_1=(-4,-1)'\), \(\mathbf x_2=(2,-1)'\) and \(\mathbf x_3=(2,2)'\), placed so that their mean, the centre, is at the origin. fig_inner <- function() { P <- tibble(id = rownames(ex3_X), x = ex3_X[, 1], y = ex3_X[, 2], b = diag(ex3_B)) P$lab <- sprintf("italic(b)[%s%s] == %d", P$id, P$id, P$b) pr <- tibble(s = c(1, 2, 1), t = c(2, 3, 3)) |> mutate(x = ex3_X[s, 1], y = ex3_X[s, 2], xend = ex3_X[t, 1], yend = ex3_X[t, 2], d2 = round(ex3_D[cbind(s, t)]^2), lab = ifelse(sqrt(d2) == round(sqrt(d2)), sprintf("italic(d)[%d%d] == %d", s, t, round(sqrt(d2))), sprintf("italic(d)[%d%d] == sqrt(%d)", s, t, d2)), lx = c(-1, 2.3, -1.25), ly = c(-1.38, 0.5, 0.95), hj = c(0.5, 0, 0.5)) ggplot() + axes0 + geom_segment(data = pr, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") + geom_text(data = pr, aes(lx, ly, label = lab, hjust = hj), parse = TRUE, size = 4.2, colour = "grey30") + geom_segment(data = P, aes(0, 0, xend = x, yend = y), colour = col_a1, linewidth = 1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed")) + geom_point(data = P, aes(x, y), size = 3, colour = "#2c3e50") + geom_text(data = P, aes(x, y, label = id), nudge_x = c(-0.3, 0.3, 0.3), nudge_y = c(0, -0.15, 0.15), size = 5, fontface = "bold", colour = "#2c3e50") + geom_text(data = P, aes(x + c(-0.3, 0.3, 0.3), y + c(-0.42, -0.55, 0.55), label = lab), parse = TRUE, size = 4, colour = col_a1, hjust = c(0.8, 0, 0)) + annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, shape = 3, size = 4, stroke = 1.2) + annotate("text", x = -0.15, y = 0.32, label = "centre", hjust = 1, size = 4, colour = "grey30") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = -5:3) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = -2:3) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-5.2, 3.9), ylim = c(-1.8, 2.9)) + labs(x = "coordinate 1", y = "coordinate 2", subtitle = expression("arrows from the centre, with squared lengths" ~ italic(b)[tt] * "; dashed: distances" ~ italic(d)[st])) } # draw the figure fig_inner() The inner product of two points multiplies their coordinates one by one and adds up the products: \[ b_{st}=\mathbf x_s'\mathbf x_t=x_{s1}x_{t1}+x_{s2}x_{t2} . \] For points 1 and 3, \(b_{13}=(-4)(2)+(-1)(2)=-10\). The inner product of a point with itself is its squared length, the squared distance from the centre: \(b_{11}=(-4)^2+(-1)^2=17\). All inner products together form the \(n\times n\) matrix \(\mathbf B\), here \[ \mathbf B=\begin{pmatrix} 17 & -7 & -10\\ -7 & 5 & 2\\ -10 & 2 & 8\end{pmatrix} . \] In matrix notation, \(\mathbf B=\mathbf X\mathbf X'\), where row \(t\) of the data matrix \(\mathbf X\) holds the coordinates of point \(t\). The inner product measures how much the arrows from the centre to two points point the same way: \(b_{st}=\lVert\mathbf x_s\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf x_t\rVert\cos\theta_{st}\), where \(\theta_{st}\) is the angle between the arrows. It is positive when they point in similar directions (points 2 and 3), negative when they point in roughly opposite directions (point 1 against points 2 and 3), and zero at a right angle. Inner products and distances are linked by the law of cosines of school geometry. Multiplying out \(d_{st}^2=(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t)'(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t)\) gives \[ d_{st}^2=b_{ss}+b_{tt}-2\,b_{st} . \] For points 1 and 3, \(d_{13}^2=17+8-2(-10)=45\), so \(d_{13}=\sqrt{45}\approx 6.7\), as in the figure. Now suppose only the distances are known. Solved for the inner product, the law of cosines reads \[ b_{st}=\tfrac12\left(b_{ss}+b_{tt}-d_{st}^2\right), \] so we need the squared lengths \(b_{tt}\) first. The centre is not in the table, but because it is the mean of the points, the squared lengths follow from the distances as well: \[ b_{tt}=\bar d^{\,2}_{t\cdot}-\tfrac12\,\bar d^{\,2}_{\cdot\cdot} , \] where \(\bar d^{\,2}_{t\cdot}\) is the average squared distance from point \(t\) to all points (the row mean of the squared distances) and \(\bar d^{\,2}_{\cdot\cdot}\) is the average over the whole table. To see why, average the law of cosines over \(s\). The \(b_{ss}\) average to the mean squared length \(\bar b\), and the \(b_{st}\) average to zero, because \(\sum_s\mathbf x_s'\mathbf x_t=(\sum_s\mathbf x_s)'\mathbf x_t\) and the points add up to the centre, \(\mathbf 0\). So \(\bar d^{\,2}_{t\cdot}=\bar b+b_{tt}\), and averaging once more over \(t\) gives \(\bar d^{\,2}_{\cdot\cdot}=2\bar b\). For the three points, square the distances and take the means: \(d_{st}^2\) \(t=1\) \(t=2\) \(t=3\) row mean \(s=1\) 0 36 45 27 \(s=2\) 36 0 9 15 \(s=3\) 45 9 0 18 The overall mean is 20. So \(b_{11}=27-10=17\), \(b_{22}=15-10=5\) and \(b_{33}=18-10=8\), and then, for example, \(b_{13}=\tfrac12(17+8-45)=-10\). Every entry of \(\mathbf B\) comes back, from the distances alone. The two steps combine into one formula, \[ b_{st}=-\tfrac12\left(d_{st}^2-\bar d^{\,2}_{s\cdot}-\bar d^{\,2}_{\cdot t}+\bar d^{\,2}_{\cdot\cdot}\right). \] In words: square the distances, subtract the row and column means, add back the overall mean, and multiply by \(-\tfrac12\). This is called double centring. In matrix form, \[ \mathbf B=-\frac12\,\mathbf J\,\mathbf D^{(2)}\mathbf J , \] where \(\mathbf D^{(2)}\) holds the squared distances (each entry squared, not the matrix product \(\mathbf D\mathbf D\)) and \(\mathbf J=I-\frac1n\mathbf 1\mathbf 1'\) subtracts means. Shifting all points changes no distance, so the table cannot know where the origin was; double centring simply puts it at the centre, the mean of the points. In R: X3 <- rbind(c(-4, -1), c(2, -1), c(2, 2)) # three points, centred D3 <- as.matrix(dist(X3)) # their distance matrix J <- diag(3) - 1/3 # subtracts means round(-0.5 * J %*% D3^2 %*% J, 10) # double centring: B from the distances ## [,1] [,2] [,3] ## [1,] 17 -7 -10 ## [2,] -7 5 2 ## [3,] -10 2 8 X3 %*% t(X3) # B from the coordinates: the same ## [,1] [,2] [,3] ## [1,] 17 -7 -10 ## [2,] -7 5 2 ## [3,] -10 2 8 5.3.2 From inner products to coordinates \(\mathbf B\) is symmetric, so it has an eigendecomposition like the covariance matrix in Chapter 4, \(\mathbf B=\mathbf VK \mathbf V'\), with the eigenvectors as the columns of \(\mathbf V\) and the eigenvalues \(\kappa_1\ge\kappa_2\ge\dots\) in the diagonal matrix \(K\). Coordinates that reproduce \(\mathbf B\) are \[ \hat{\mathbf X}=\mathbf VK^{1/2},\qquad\text{since}\qquad \hat{\mathbf X}\hat{\mathbf X}'=\mathbf VK^{1/2}K^{1/2}\mathbf V'=\mathbf B . \] Since \(\mathbf B\) comes from \(\mathbf D\) alone, this is how the maps of this chapter were made from the distances only: double centring gives \(\mathbf B\), and its eigendecomposition gives the coordinates. But \(\hat{\mathbf X}\) is not the only answer. Turn it with any rotation or reflection \(Q\), so that \(Q'Q=I\). The turned coordinates \(\hat{\mathbf X}Q\) give \[ (\hat{\mathbf X}Q)(\hat{\mathbf X}Q)'=\hat{\mathbf X}QQ'\hat{\mathbf X}'=\hat{\mathbf X}\hat{\mathbf X}'=\mathbf B , \] the same inner products, and so the same distances. Geometrically, turning the points around the centre changes neither the lengths of the arrows nor the angles between them. So the coordinates are identified only up to a rotation or reflection, as the maps of the states in Section 5.2 showed. Each eigenvalue gives one dimension of the map. Distances computed from \(p\) coordinates give at most \(p\) positive eigenvalues, and the rest are zero. For the three points, the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf B\) are 25.8, 4.2 and 0. For the states, the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf B\) are 76,952,297 and 12,861,163, followed by zeros, so two dimensions rebuild the table exactly. To draw a map in \(k\) dimensions, keep the \(k\) largest eigenvalues. In R: us_mds <- cmdscale(us_D, k = 2, eig = TRUE) # classical MDS, two dimensions head(round(us_mds$points), 3) # the rebuilt coordinates (km) ## [,1] [,2] ## AL 394 736 ## AZ -1752 628 ## AR -92 515 round(us_mds$eig[1:4]) # the eigenvalues of B: two positive, the rest zero ## [1] 76952297 12861163 0 0 5.3.3 Which map MDS returns: the principal component scores All turned maps \(\hat{\mathbf X}Q\) fit the distances equally well, so which one does classical MDS return? Its coordinates \(\mathbf VK^{1/2}\) have a special property. They have mean zero, since the map is centred, and their covariance matrix is \[ \frac{1}{n-1}\hat{\mathbf X}'\hat{\mathbf X}=\frac{1}{n-1}K^{1/2}\mathbf V'\mathbf VK^{1/2}=\frac{1}{n-1}K , \] because the eigenvectors are perpendicular and have length one (\(\mathbf V'\mathbf V=I\)). This matrix is diagonal. So the coordinates of the MDS map are uncorrelated, and dimension \(l\) has the variance \(\kappa_l/(n-1)\): the first dimension carries the most spread, the second the most of what is left, and so on. Turning the map would mix the coordinates and make them correlated. The slider in Section 5.2 shows it. The correlation of the two coordinates is zero only when the map lines up with the long and the short axis of the country (at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270°), and dimension 1 carries the largest share of the spread only at 0° and 180°, where it runs along the long axis. This is exactly the rule by which PCA chooses its rotation in Chapter 4: the principal component scores are uncorrelated, the first has the largest variance, the second the largest of what is left, and so on. So MDS and PCA line up the points in the same way and return the same coordinates. Only the sign of each column is open, since flipping a column keeps the coordinates uncorrelated and their variances unchanged; that is why the states came out upside down. The algebra confirms this. Write the coordinates as in Chapter 4, \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma\mathbf f_t\), with the rotation \(\Gamma\) and the principal component scores \(\mathbf f_t\). In rows, \(\mathbf X=\mathbf F\Gamma'\), where row \(t\) of \(\mathbf F\) holds the scores \(\mathbf f_t'\). Then \[ \mathbf B=\mathbf X\mathbf X'=\mathbf F\Gamma'\Gamma\mathbf F'=\mathbf F\mathbf F' : \] the rotation cancels. The scores have mean zero and are uncorrelated, with the variances \(\delta_l^2\) of Chapter 4, so \(\mathbf F'\mathbf F=(n-1)\Delta^2\) is diagonal. Hence \(\mathbf B\mathbf F=\mathbf F(\mathbf F'\mathbf F)=(n-1)\,\mathbf F\Delta^2\): each column of \(\mathbf F\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf B\), with the eigenvalue \((n-1)\delta_l^2\), \(n-1\) times the variance of the scores. Scaled to length one, the columns of \(\mathbf F\) are the columns of \(\mathbf V\), so \(\mathbf VK^{1/2}=\mathbf F\): Classical MDS of Euclidean distances returns the principal component scores of the coordinates (up to the signs of the columns): the orientation in which the coordinates are uncorrelated, with the largest variance first. This is why it is also called principal coordinates analysis (Gower 1966). For the three points, PCA of the coordinates and MDS of the distances give the same map, up to signs: round(prcomp(X3)$x, 3) # PCA scores of the three points ## PC1 PC2 ## [1,] -4.118 0.202 ## [2,] 1.624 -1.537 ## [3,] 2.494 1.335 round(cmdscale(D3, k = 2), 3) # classical MDS of their distances: the same, up to signs ## [,1] [,2] ## 1 4.118 0.202 ## 2 -1.624 -1.537 ## 3 -2.494 1.335 That is why the rebuilt map of the states lies flat: its first dimension is the direction of greatest spread, the long east-west axis of the country, as PCA would choose. The same holds with more variables. MDS of the Euclidean distances between the 50 states on the six standardised indicators of Chapter 4 (distances between their profiles, not their locations; Section 5.6 looks at them) returns their first two principal component scores, up to rounding errors (5e-14). Starting from a distance matrix, the natural route has two steps: Rebuild a map from \(\mathbf D\). This needs facts from outside the table, such as where the middle is and which way is north (Section 5.2). Choose \(A\) on that map, as in Chapter 4. The distances fix the shape of the cloud, but not which way each variable points in it. So step 1 is needed only if step 2 has to know which axis is which variable. 5.4.1 PCA needs no first step Suppose step 1 had turned the map by some rotation \(Q\), giving the coordinates \(Q\mathbf x_t\) instead of \(\mathbf x_t\). Their covariance matrix is \(QSQ'=(Q\Gamma)\Delta^2(Q\Gamma)'\), so PCA finds the directions \(Q\Gamma\) and the scores \[ (Q\Gamma)'Q\mathbf x_t=\Gamma'Q'Q\mathbf x_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t=\mathbf f_t , \] the same as before. Whatever orientation step 1 picks, step 2 turns it back, and a reflection changes nothing either, since \(Q'Q=I\) is all the argument uses. The slider chooses the orientation of step 1 (left), and the PCA scores of step 2 (right) do not move: us_scores <- function(X) { # PCA scores, signs fixed (Maine positive on both) p <- prcomp(X); Fs <- p$x sg <- sign(Fs["ME", ]); sweep(Fs, 2, sg, "*") } fig_two_steps <- function(step = 15, titles = c("Step 1: coordinates, in some orientation", "Step 2: their PCA scores"), slider = "orientation chosen in step 1: ") { angs <- seq(0, 360 - step, by = step) fr <- purrr::map(angs, function(a) { Q <- rotation_matrix(a * pi / 180) Xa <- us_X %*% Q; Fa <- us_scores(Xa) Ga <- solve(crossprod(Xa), crossprod(Xa, Fa)) # the PCA rotation for these coordinates Oa <- us_outline %*% Q; OF <- Oa %*% Ga list(pts = tibble(x = c(Xa[, 1], Fa[, 1]), y = c(Xa[, 2], Fa[, 2]), lab = rep(us48$abb, 2), panel = rep(c("map", "scores"), each = nrow(Xa)), k = a), out = tibble(x = c(Oa[, 1], OF[, 1]), y = c(Oa[, 2], OF[, 2]), panel = rep(c("map", "scores"), each = nrow(Oa)), k = a)) }) pts <- bind_rows(purrr::map(fr, "pts")); out <- bind_rows(purrr::map(fr, "out")) one <- function(pn, col) plot_ly() |> add_trace(data = filter(out, panel == pn), x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~k, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = "#bbbbbb", width = 1.2), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) |> add_trace(data = filter(pts, panel == pn), x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~k, text = ~lab, type = "scatter", mode = "text", textfont = list(size = 9, color = col), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) ax <- function(t) list(title = t, range = c(-3000, 3000), zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#e5e5e5") subplot(one("map", "#2c3e50"), one("scores", col_a1), margin = 0.06, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |> layout(xaxis = ax("coordinate 1 (km)"), yaxis = c(ax("coordinate 2 (km)"), scaleanchor = "x"), xaxis2 = ax("PCA score 1 (km)"), yaxis2 = c(ax("PCA score 2 (km)"), scaleanchor = "x2"), margin = list(t = 80), annotations = list( list(x = 0.235, y = 1.02, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "center", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(size = 14), text = titles[1]), list(x = 0.765, y = 1.02, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "center", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(size = 14), text = titles[2]))) |> animation_opts(frame = 150, transition = 0, redraw = TRUE) |> animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = slider, suffix = "°")) |> animation_button(label = "Play") |> finalize_animation(list(), start_frame = "0", prefix = slider, suffix = "°") } # draw the figure fig_two_steps() So classical MDS skips step 1 and goes straight from \(\mathbf D\) to the scores (Section 5.3). Only the assumptions of PCA remain: the first dimension has the largest variance, the next the largest of the rest, and so on, with the sign of each dimension left open. The loop road has no map to rebuild at all, since travel times along a road are not straight-line distances, and MDS still goes straight to its latent coordinates, the ring. 5.4.2 The roommates need no first step either The roommates of Chapter 4 were paired at random, so they have no order. Swapping them must therefore leave the cloud of their GPA pairs unchanged, and the line halfway between their two GPA axes must be an axis of symmetry of the cloud. So the GPA axes lie at 45° to the axes of the cloud, and the map that MDS returns shows them: fig_room_axes <- function() { E <- t(ellipse_xy(diag(room_sd), r = 2)) ax <- tibble(xend = 1.25 / sqrt(2) * c(1, 1), yend = 1.25 / sqrt(2) * c(1, -1), lab = c("roommate 1's GPA", "roommate 2's GPA"), vj = c(0, 1)) arc <- function(a0, a1, r = 0.42) { t <- seq(a0, a1, length.out = 30); tibble(x = r * cos(t), y = r * sin(t)) } ggplot() + axes0 + geom_point(data = tibble(x = room_map[, 1], y = room_map[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.55, size = 1.3) + geom_path(data = tibble(x = E[, 1], y = E[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "#2c3e50", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_path(data = arc(0, pi / 4), aes(x, y), colour = col_a2, linewidth = 0.6) + geom_path(data = arc(-pi / 4, 0), aes(x, y), colour = col_a2, linewidth = 0.6) + annotate("text", x = 0.6 * cos(c(pi / 8, -pi / 8)), y = 0.6 * sin(c(pi / 8, -pi / 8)), label = "45°", size = 3.8, colour = col_a2) + geom_segment(data = ax, aes(0, 0, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1.1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed")) + geom_text(data = ax, aes(xend + 0.04, yend, label = lab, vjust = vj), hjust = 0, size = 4.2, colour = col_a2, fontface = "bold") + annotate("text", x = 2.15, y = 0.04, label = "long axis:\nboth GPAs rise", hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = 3.6, colour = "grey35", lineheight = 0.9) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.65, 2.15), ylim = c(-1.15, 1.15)) + labs(x = "first dimension of the MDS map", y = "second dimension", title = "The MDS map of 200 pairs of roommates", subtitle = "No order: the two GPA axes lie at 45° to the axes of the cloud") + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12), axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) } # draw the figure fig_room_axes() The rest follows from the two standard deviations of the map, the principal component standard deviations \(\delta_1=0.6\) and \(\delta_2=0.4\). In GPA coordinates, the axes of the cloud point along \((1,1)'/\sqrt2\), where both GPAs rise, and \((1,-1)'/\sqrt2\). With \(\Gamma\) the matrix of these two columns and \(\Delta=\operatorname{diag}(\delta_1,\delta_2)\), the covariance matrix is \(S=\Gamma\Delta^2\Gamma'\), and its symmetric root is \[ A=\Gamma\Delta\,\Gamma'=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}\delta_1+\delta_2&\delta_1-\delta_2\\ \delta_1-\delta_2&\delta_1+\delta_2\end{pmatrix}, \] since this \(A\) is symmetric and \(AA'=\Gamma\Delta^2\Gamma'=S\). With ones on the diagonal of \(C\) (Section 4.1), the peer effect is \[ c_{12}=c_{21}=\frac{a_{12}}{a_{22}}=\frac{\delta_1-\delta_2}{\delta_1+\delta_2}=\frac{0.6-0.4}{0.6+0.4}=0.20 , \] the value of Chapter 4, from the distances alone. As with PCA, starting from \(\mathbf D\) adds no assumption: “neither roommate comes first” is the assumption the symmetric root makes anyway. The distances fix the size of the peer effect, though not its sign. They cannot tell whether both GPAs rise along the long axis of the cloud, as drawn, or along the short one, which would mean that the roommates hurt each other. 5.4.3 When the first step is needed A first step is needed when step 2 has an order, that is, when it must know which axis is which variable. Cholesky always has one, since the regressor comes first. A structural restriction names a particular variable, such as the manual’s fuel flow for the headwind. And the roommates would have an order if one of them came first, say a senior paired with a first-year student. Their GPAs would then differ in how much they vary, their axes could lie at any angle to the axes of the cloud, and every angle would give different peer effects. In each case, information from outside the table must turn the map into place before step 2 can start. A first step is needed only when step 2 must know which axis is which variable. PCA never needs it, and neither do the roommates, who have no order. From a table of distances, classical MDS goes straight to latent coordinates, with the assumptions of PCA alone. PCA the symmetric root for roommates paired at random Cholesky none of them Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 a. 4 c. 5.5 Distances learned from text: embeddings 5.5.1 From words to vectors The same idea is at the heart of how AI models handle language. A computer cannot calculate with words, so before any learning the text is split into tokens (words or pieces of words, by a tokenizer), and each token of a vocabulary of \(n\) tokens is turned into a vector. This step is the encoding. The simplest version is one-hot encoding: token number \(t\) becomes a one-hot vector, a list of \(n\) numbers with a 1 in place \(t\) and zeros everywhere else (the \(t\)-th unit vector; “one-hot” because exactly one entry is switched on). With three words, \[ \text{coke}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \text{pepsi}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \text{runway}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}. \] These vectors live in a Euclidean space, but its geometry says nothing: every two different words are the same distance \(\sqrt2\) apart, so “coke” is as far from “pepsi” as from “runway”. Meaning has to come from data. This is the difference between an encoding and an embedding. An encoding describes each object by numbers. An embedding places the objects so that closeness in the space means something. The loop road shows the difference. The position along the road in minutes from the start, one number per place, is an encoding: the Church (minute 1) and the Stadium (minute 36) are far apart as numbers, but only 7 minutes apart by road. The ring that MDS drew is an embedding: places that are close by road are close on it. The one-hot vectors of the words are an encoding as well, and the task is to turn them into an embedding. 5.5.2 Distances from text A language model is trained on huge amounts of text, and from it, it learns which words go together. The simplest way to turn “go together” into a distance is to measure it in the text itself: two words are close if they usually appear near each other, and far apart if they rarely do. For words \(s\) and \(t\), go to every place in the text where \(s\) appears, count how many words away the nearest \(t\) is, and average over all those places. Do the same from \(t\) to \(s\) and take the mean of the two. The result, \(d_{st}\), is the average distance between the two words in the text, counted in words. Words that often follow each other, the pairs a language model learns to predict, are only one or two words apart. A small example makes this concrete. Take a made-up text of 4,339 words, written with 18 words from three themes of this course: drinks, flights and campus life (think of a real text with all other words removed). It comes in paragraphs on one theme each, and now and then students and pilots drink coffee. It starts like this: writeLines(strwrap(paste(word_text[1:40], collapse = " "), width = 100)) ## tea cup coffee tea coke sugar pepsi coke cup coke sugar sugar coke airport runway plane fuel fuel ## headwind plane fuel plane fuel airport pilot plane fuel plane exam grade exam student student ## roommate exam exam roommate grade student exam Measured over the whole text, “coke” and “pepsi” are on average 3.2 words apart, and “coke” and “runway” 22.6. The average distances of all pairs of words form a distance matrix \(\mathbf D\), just like the travel times of the loop road: fig_word_D <- function(title = TRUE) { lev <- word_vocab d <- as_tibble(as.table(word_D), .name_repair = ~ c("w1", "w2", "d")) |> mutate(w1 = factor(w1, levels = rev(lev)), w2 = factor(w2, levels = lev)) ggplot(d, aes(w2, w1, fill = d)) + geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#08306b", high = "#f7fbff", name = "words\napart") + coord_equal() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = if (title) expression("Distance matrix" ~ bold(D) * ": the average distance" ~ italic(d)[ij] ~ "in the text, in words")) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1, colour = col_th[word_theme[lev]]), axis.text.y = element_text(colour = rev(col_th[word_theme[lev]])), panel.grid = element_blank()) } # draw the figure fig_word_D() 5.5.3 The embedding Classical MDS of this distance matrix gives each word a set of coordinates. In machine learning, these coordinates are the word’s embedding, the number of dimensions is the embedding dimension, and the space they live in is the embedding space (or latent space). Closeness in the embedding space means that the words usually appear near each other: fig_word_map <- function() { d <- tibble(word = word_vocab, x = word_Y[, 1], y = word_Y[, 2], theme = word_theme[word_vocab]) ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = theme)) + axes0 + geom_point(size = 2.4) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = word), size = 4.2, seed = 3, show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = 30, box.padding = 0.35) + scale_colour_manual(values = col_th, name = "theme\n(not used\nby MDS)") + coord_equal() + labs(x = "embedding dimension 1", y = "embedding dimension 2") } # draw the figure fig_word_map() MDS was never told the themes (the colours), yet each theme forms its own group. “Coffee” sits between the drinks and the other two themes, because in this text students and pilots drink coffee too. The dictionary between the two languages: MDS machine learning object (a word) token distance matrix \(\mathbf D\) average distances between words in a lot of text small distance \(d_{st}\) usually near each other coordinates of one object its embedding vector number of dimensions \(k\) embedding dimension the map embedding space, latent space any rotation fits equally well the axes of an embedding need not mean anything on their own 5.5.4 What real models do Real models do not run classical MDS on a table of word pairs. They learn the embeddings while training a neural network to predict words from their neighbours (word2vec, Mikolov et al. 2013) or to predict the next token (the large language models behind today’s AI chatbots). Their training loss, the cross-entropy, is the average “surprise” \(-\log P\) of the word that actually comes next, so a model that has learned which words go together is rarely surprised. The embedding layer is an \(n\times k\) table, with one row for each of the \(n\) tokens in the vocabulary and one column for each of the \(k\) embedding dimensions; row \(t\) is the embedding of token \(t\): multiplying the one-hot vector of token \(t\) by this table picks out row \(t\), so the layer replaces the one-hot vector by a vector learned from data. The embedding dimension is a few hundred for word2vec and runs to many thousands for large language models (12,288 for GPT-3). The goal is the same as here, though: coordinates whose geometry reproduces how words are used. For word2vec this can be made precise. Its training amounts to factorising a table that says, for each pair of words, how much more often they occur together than they would by chance, on a log scale (Levy and Goldberg 2014), much as classical MDS factorises \(\mathbf B\). Directions can carry meaning too: in word2vec, “king” \(-\) “man” \(+\) “woman” lands close to “queen”. To look at a learned embedding, people project it to two dimensions, with PCA or MDS or with non-linear relatives such as t-SNE and UMAP. And the rotation problem of this chapter applies too. Turning the whole embedding space changes no distance, so the axes of an embedding need not mean anything by themselves; the distances and directions between words do. Any measure of how different two observations are will do, and the choice depends on the data: distance between \(s\) and \(t\) typical use Euclidean \(\sqrt{\sum_j (x_{sj}-x_{tj})^2}\) coordinates in the same units standardised Euclidean Euclidean on standardised variables variables in different units (Chapter 2) Mahalanobis \(\sqrt{(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t)'S^{-1}(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t)}\) relative to the shape of the cloud (Section 2.6.2) Manhattan (city block) \(\sum_j \lvert x_{sj}-x_{tj}\rvert\) walking a grid of streets; less driven by one large difference great circle along the surface of the Earth places on the globe travel time along a road network the loop road share of mismatches share of yes/no variables on which \(s\) and \(t\) differ binary data, such as votes judged dissimilarity a rating, such as 1 (alike) to 9 (different) perceptions, tastes distance in a text average number of words between them words 5.6.2 The states under three distances So far, the states were places, and their distances were kilometres. A distance matrix can just as well say how different the states are in other respects. Take the six indicators of Chapter 4: income, illiteracy, life expectancy, murder rate, high-school graduation and days of frost, standardised as there. Each state is then a point in a six-dimensional space, with one coordinate per indicator, and the Euclidean distance of Section 5.2 works the same way with six coordinates instead of two: \[ d_{st}=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{6}(z_{sj}-z_{tj})^2} , \] where \(z_{sj}\) is the standardised value of indicator \(j\) for state \(s\). This distance compares the profiles of two states, how rich, how educated, how safe and how cold they are, and not their locations. Four states show the difference: round(X6[st_ex, ], 1) # the six indicators, before standardising ## Income Illiteracy LifeExp Murder HSGrad Frost ## Montana 4347 0.6 70.6 5.0 59.2 155 ## New Hampshire 4281 0.7 71.2 3.3 57.6 174 ## California 5114 1.1 71.7 10.3 62.6 20 ## Nevada 5149 0.5 69.0 11.5 65.2 188 round(st_D$Euclidean[st_ex, st_ex], 2) # distances between the standardised profiles ## Montana New Hampshire California Nevada ## Montana 0.00 0.82 3.46 2.66 ## New Hampshire 0.82 0.00 3.89 3.27 ## California 3.46 3.89 0.00 3.95 ## Nevada 2.66 3.27 3.95 0.00 Montana and New Hampshire lie 2,971 km apart, yet their profiles are only 0.82 apart: just 1% of all 1,225 pairs of states are more alike. California and Nevada are neighbours, 384 km apart, yet their profiles are 3.95 apart, more than the 3.00 of a typical pair: Nevada has less illiteracy, a lower life expectancy and far more days of frost. Classical MDS turns such a table into a map of the profiles, on which states with similar profiles end up close, wherever they lie. Here are the maps from three distance tables, all computed from the same six indicators: the Euclidean distance above, the Manhattan distance and the Mahalanobis distance (the second and third maps turned to line up with the first): fig_states_maps <- function() { ref <- st_mds$Euclidean$points if (ref["Alaska", 2] < 0) ref[, 2] <- -ref[, 2] ttl <- c(Euclidean = "Euclidean", Manhattan = "Manhattan (city block)", Mahalanobis = "Mahalanobis") sub <- c(Euclidean = "= the PCA scores of Chapter 4", Manhattan = "sum of absolute differences", Mahalanobis = "relative to the shape of the cloud") panels <- lapply(names(st_D), function(nm) { Y <- if (nm == "Euclidean") ref else procrustes_align(st_mds[[nm]]$points, ref) d <- tibble(x = Y[, 1], y = Y[, 2], lab = state.abb) ggplot(d, aes(x, y, label = lab)) + axes0 + geom_text(size = 2.6, colour = "#2c3e50") + coord_equal() + labs(title = ttl[[nm]], subtitle = sub[[nm]], x = "dimension 1", y = "dimension 2") + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10)) }) wrap_plots(panels, nrow = 1) } # draw the figure fig_states_maps() The Euclidean map is the map of principal component scores of Chapter 4, the points of its biplot. The Manhattan map looks much the same, with the states spread a little differently. The Mahalanobis map is round: measuring distance relative to the shape of the cloud removes the correlations, so every direction carries the same variance. The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf B\) show the difference. Each state now has six coordinates, one per indicator, so \(\mathbf B\) can have up to six positive eigenvalues (the flat map of the states had two coordinates, and so two). Here are the first seven for each table: sapply(st_D, function(D) round(mds_eigen(D)[1:7], 1)) # the seven largest eigenvalues of B ## Euclidean Manhattan Mahalanobis ## [1,] 174.2 965.0 49 ## [2,] 48.4 193.3 49 ## [3,] 38.7 172.9 49 ## [4,] 15.7 83.8 49 ## [5,] 10.1 50.4 49 ## [6,] 6.8 33.6 49 ## [7,] 0.0 29.1 0 Euclidean: six positive eigenvalues, then zeros. They are \(n-1=49\) times the variances of the six principal components of Chapter 4, so two dimensions keep 76%, the share of variance of the first two components. Manhattan: more than six nonzero eigenvalues, 25 of them negative. Manhattan distances are not Euclidean (Section 5.6.3). Mahalanobis: six positive eigenvalues, all equal to 49. The Mahalanobis distance between two states is the Euclidean distance between their standardised scores \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) of Chapter 4, which have variance one in every direction, and \(n-1\) times a variance of one is 49. So two dimensions keep only two sixths, 33%, and not even PCA’s assumption can say which two directions to show: MDS returns the standardised scores in an arbitrary rotation. The round cloud of shocks in the Introduction had the same problem. This goes one step beyond PCA of the correlation matrix, which gives the Euclidean map here: standardising gives every variable a variance of one, and the Mahalanobis distance also removes the correlations, which gives every component a variance of one. 5.6.3 Distances that no map reproduces Euclidean distances always fit some set of points exactly. Many other distances do not: no set of points, in any number of dimensions, has them as straight-line distances. A loop shows why. Take four places evenly spaced around a loop, A, B, C and D. Along the road, neighbours are 1 minute apart and opposite places 2 minutes (top left). Can four points on a map have these as straight-line distances? fig_loop4 <- function(nrow = 2) { ttl <- theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10.5, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30", lineheight = 1.05)) ang <- c(A = 180, B = 90, C = 0, D = 270) * pi / 180 mid <- c(135, 45, 315, 225) * pi / 180 # directions of the side midpoints A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A lim <- coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.45, 1.45), ylim = c(-1.45, 1.45), clip = "off") corners <- function(P) list( geom_point(data = P, aes(x, y), size = 3, colour = "#2c3e50"), geom_text(data = P, aes(x * (1 + 0.28 / sqrt(x^2 + y^2)), y * (1 + 0.28 / sqrt(x^2 + y^2)), label = lab), size = 5, fontface = "bold", colour = "#2c3e50")) # 1: the table, distances along the loop r <- 0.85 P1 <- tibble(lab = names(ang), x = r * cos(ang), y = r * sin(ang)) circ <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 300), x = r * cos(t), y = r * sin(t)) p1 <- ggplot() + geom_path(data = circ, aes(x, y), colour = "#cccccc", linewidth = 3) + corners(P1) + annotate("text", x = 1.3 * r * cos(mid), y = 1.3 * r * sin(mid), label = "1 min", size = 3.8, colour = "grey35") + lim + theme_void() + ttl + labs(title = "The table", subtitle = "along the loop: neighbours 1 minute apart,\nopposite places 2 minutes") # 4: why no arrangement in any number of dimensions works p4 <- ggplot() + annotate("segment", x = -1, xend = 1, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = "#2c3e50", linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("point", x = c(-1, 1), y = 0, size = 3, colour = "#2c3e50") + annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, size = 3.4, colour = col_a2) + annotate("text", x = c(-1.12, 1.12), y = 0, label = c("A", "C"), size = 5, fontface = "bold", colour = "#2c3e50", hjust = c(1, 0)) + annotate("text", x = 0, y = c(0.2, -0.2), label = c("B", "D"), size = 5, fontface = "bold", colour = col_a2) + annotate("text", x = c(-0.5, 0.5), y = 0.12, label = "1", size = 4.2, colour = "grey35") + annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.85, size = 3.9, colour = "grey20", lineheight = 1.05, label = "B and D would be the same point,\nyet they are 2 minutes apart.") + lim + theme_void() + ttl + labs(title = "Why nothing works", subtitle = "A to B to C takes 1 + 1 = 2, as A to C does.\nSo B sits halfway along the line, and so does D.") wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3, p4, nrow = nrow) } # draw the figure fig_loop4() A square is the natural try, but it cannot get all six distances right. With sides of 1, the diagonals are only \(\sqrt2\approx 1.41\), not 2 (top right). Classical MDS returns the square with diagonals of 2, and then the sides are 1.41, not 1 (bottom left). No other arrangement does better, not even in three or more dimensions (bottom right). The trip from A to C through B takes 1 + 1 = 2 minutes, exactly as long as the direct trip. For straight lines, a detour costs nothing only when B lies on the straight line from A to C, halfway along; anywhere else, the direct line is shorter (the triangle inequality). The same holds for D. So B and D would be the same point, the midpoint between A and C, yet the table puts them 2 minutes apart. (The four corners of a city block, one block apart, have the same table of Manhattan distances.) Classical MDS detects this through the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mathbf B\). For any coordinates, \(\mathbf B=\mathbf X\mathbf X'\). If \(\mathbf v\) is an eigenvector, \(\mathbf B\mathbf v=\kappa\mathbf v\), then \(\kappa\,\mathbf v'\mathbf v=\mathbf v'\mathbf X\mathbf X'\mathbf v=\lVert\mathbf X'\mathbf v\rVert^2\) is never negative, so a negative eigenvalue of \(\mathbf B\) means that no coordinates reproduce the table. For the four places, the eigenvalues are 2, 2, 0 and \(-1\): the two eigenvalues of 2 give the square of the bottom-left panel, and the \(-1\) is the part of the table that no map reproduces. The test works both ways: if \(\mathbf B\) has no negative eigenvalues, \(\mathbf VK^{1/2}\) reproduces the table exactly, in as many dimensions as there are positive eigenvalues (Schoenberg 1935). When there are negative eigenvalues, classical MDS drops them: a negative eigenvalue has no real square root, so it cannot become a column of \(\mathbf VK^{1/2}\). The bars show the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf B\) for five tables (relative to the largest; red ones are negative): D_wait <- function(w) { # travel times (minutes) with a wait of w minutes at the site a <- abs(outer(s_min, s_min, "-")) D <- pmin(a, T_loop - a + w) dimnames(D) <- list(places$place, places$place); D } eig_table <- function() { sets <- list( "US map, flat (Euclidean)" = us_D, "US, great circle" = us_G, "States, Manhattan" = st_D$Manhattan, "Loop road, no waiting" = D_wait(0), "Words, average distance" = word_D) purrr::imap_dfr(sets, function(D, nm) { ev <- mds_eigen(D) tibble(set = nm, j = seq_along(ev), ev = ev, rel = ev / ev[1]) }) |> mutate(set = factor(set, levels = names(sets))) } fig_eigen_types <- function() { d <- eig_table() brk <- function(l) { b <- pretty(c(1, l[2]), n = 4); c(1, b[b > 1 & b <= l[2]]) } ggplot(d, aes(j, rel, fill = rel < -1e-8)) + geom_col(width = 0.75) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") + facet_wrap(~ set, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") + scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = col_a1, `TRUE` = col_a2), labels = c("positive", "negative"), name = NULL) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = brk) + labs(x = "eigenvalue number, largest first (all of them)", y = "eigenvalue / largest eigenvalue") + theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")) } # draw the figure fig_eigen_types() The flat map of the states (Euclidean): two positive eigenvalues, the rest zero. Great-circle distances between the same state centres, measured along the curved surface of the Earth: two large eigenvalues, a small third one and negative ones too small to see (more on these below). Manhattan distances between the states: 25 small negative eigenvalues. Travel times on the loop road without waiting, for the reason shown above: large negative eigenvalues. Average distances between the words: 6 small negative eigenvalues. The great-circle distances deserve a closer look. The state centres now lie on the curved surface of the Earth, and their MDS map needs a third dimension: its eigenvalue is 0.1% of the first. In the figure, each state sits at its first two MDS coordinates, which give the familiar map, and its colour shows the third coordinate: red states lie above the plane of the first two dimensions, blue ones below it. The middle of the country bulges up by up to 63 km, and the edges bend down by up to 120 km, as on a globe: fig_us_sphere <- function(title = TRUE) { Y <- us_mds_G$points Y2 <- procrustes_align(Y[, 1:2], us_X) d <- tibble(x = Y2[, 1], y = Y2[, 2], z = us_bulge, lab = us48$abb) ggplot() + geom_path(data = us_borders, aes(east, north, group = group), colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) + geom_label(data = d, aes(x, y, label = lab, fill = z), size = 2.5, label.size = 0, colour = "white", fontface = "bold", label.padding = unit(0.12, "lines")) + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "#bbbbbb", high = "#b2182b", name = "dimension 3 (km)\nred: above the plane\nblue: below it") + coord_equal(xlim = c(-2900, 2900), ylim = c(-2100, 2100)) + labs(x = "dimension 1 (km)", y = "dimension 2 (km)", title = if (title) "Classical MDS of the great-circle distances between the state centres", subtitle = if (title) "position: dimensions 1 and 2 (the familiar map); colour: dimension 3, the bulge of the Earth") + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10.5)) } # draw the figure fig_us_sphere() Straight through the Earth, the distances between the state centres (the chords) would be exactly Euclidean, the distances between points in three dimensions. Along the surface of the Earth, a sphere with a radius of 6,371 km, an arc of \(d\) km is longer than its chord by about \(d^3/(24\cdot 6371^2)\) km: 82 km for the longest trip, from Maine to California (4,300 km). No map reproduces that excess, and it makes the small negative eigenvalues. So a map from classical MDS can miss the table for two different reasons. Dropping positive eigenvalues, to draw fewer dimensions than the table needs, is dimension reduction, as in PCA. Dropping negative eigenvalues is unavoidable: no number of extra dimensions brings them back. With a few small negative eigenvalues, MDS still gives a useful map from the positive ones. With many large ones, the straight-line distances of a map are a poor model for the table, and non-metric MDS (Section 5.8) is often the better choice. In R, cmdscale() keeps only positive eigenvalues: asked for more dimensions than there are positive eigenvalues, it warns and returns fewer. (Older versions of R, as in the output printed by Everitt and Hothorn, show NaN for those dimensions instead.) These travel times are the straight-line distances of the corners of a square in the plane the corners of a regular tetrahedron no set of points, in any number of dimensions four points on a line Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 a. 4 c (in a square the diagonal is \(\sqrt2\), not 2). 5.7 How many dimensions, and how good is the map? 5.7.1 The share of the eigenvalues As in PCA, each eigenvalue says how much one dimension contributes, so the first \(k\) dimensions keep the share \[ \frac{\kappa_1+\dots+\kappa_k}{\kappa_1+\dots+\kappa_n} \] of the eigenvalues. For Euclidean distances this is the share of variance of Chapter 4: two dimensions keep 100% for the flat map of the states, and 76% for the six state indicators. With negative eigenvalues the plain share can exceed one (for the loop road it is 122%), so Everitt and Hothorn, following Mardia, Kent and Bibby (1979), use the absolute values or the squares of the eigenvalues instead, and look for values above about 0.8. For the loop road without waiting, two dimensions keep 71% of the absolute values and 93% of the squares; for the words, 90% and 100%. The eigenvalues also tell the story of the construction site. As the wait grows, the largest eigenvalue grows and the others shrink. At 27.9 minutes all but the largest have vanished, the negative ones included: from then on the travel times are distances along a line, which one dimension reproduces exactly. D_wait <- function(w) { # travel times (minutes) with a wait of w minutes at the site a <- abs(outer(s_min, s_min, "-")) D <- pmin(a, T_loop - a + w) dimnames(D) <- list(places$place, places$place); D } fig_loop_eigen <- function() { ws <- seq(0, 40, by = 0.5) d <- purrr::map_dfr(ws, function(w) { ev <- mds_eigen(D_wait(w)) tibble(w = w, which = c("largest", "second", "third", "smallest (most negative)"), ev = c(ev[1], ev[2], ev[3], min(ev[length(ev)], 0))) }) |> mutate(which = factor(which, levels = c("largest", "second", "third", "smallest (most negative)"))) ggplot(d, aes(w, ev, colour = which)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_vline(xintercept = w_star, linetype = "22", colour = col_wait) + annotate("text", x = w_star + 0.6, y = 900, label = sprintf("%.1f min:\nnobody drives\nthrough", w_star), hjust = 0, size = 3.6, colour = col_wait) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(largest = col_a1, second = col_a2, third = "#7b4fb5", `smallest (most negative)` = "grey35"), name = NULL) + labs(x = "waiting time at the construction site (minutes)", y = expression("eigenvalue of"~bold(B))) + theme(legend.position = "right") } # draw the figure fig_loop_eigen() 5.7.2 The Shepard diagram A direct check plots each distance on the map against the distance in the table: a Shepard diagram. For a perfect map, all points lie on the diagonal. D_wait <- function(w) { # travel times (minutes) with a wait of w minutes at the site a <- abs(outer(s_min, s_min, "-")) D <- pmin(a, T_loop - a + w) dimnames(D) <- list(places$place, places$place); D } shepard_df <- function(D, Y, nm) { dm <- as.matrix(dist(Y)); i <- which(upper.tri(D)) tibble(set = nm, obs = D[i], map = dm[i]) } fig_shepard <- function() { d <- bind_rows( shepard_df(us_D, us_mds$points, "US map (2 of 2 dimensions)"), shepard_df(st_D$Euclidean, st_mds$Euclidean$points, "States, 6 variables (2 dimensions)"), shepard_df(D_wait(0), cmdscale(as.dist(D_wait(0)), k = 2), "Loop road (2 dimensions)"), shepard_df(word_D, word_mds$points, "Words (2 dimensions)")) |> mutate(set = factor(set, levels = unique(set))) ggplot(d, aes(obs, map)) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = col_a2, linetype = "22") + geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.1, colour = "#2c3e50") + facet_wrap(~ set, nrow = 1, scales = "free") + labs(x = "distance in the table", y = "distance on the map") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")) } # draw the figure fig_shepard() The flat map of the states is perfect. For the six state indicators, two dimensions shrink the distances, never stretch them: what is dropped is the spread along the other four components (Section 4.7). For the loop road it is the other way round: every distance on the map is longer than in the table. Each squared distance adds up contributions from all dimensions, \(d_{st}^2=\sum_l\kappa_l(v_{sl}-v_{tl})^2\), and the dropped dimensions include the negative eigenvalues, which subtract. The words, whose few negative eigenvalues are small, lie close to the diagonal. Check your understanding For Euclidean distances, the share of the first \(k\) eigenvalues is the share of variance kept by \(k\) principal components always one the stress the largest distance In a Shepard diagram of a perfect map, the points lie on a horizontal line lie on the diagonal form a ring are spread at random Answers 1 a. 2 b. 5.8 When only the order counts: non-metric MDS Sometimes only the order of the distances can be trusted. A person rating how different two leaders are on a scale from 1 to 9 can say that one pair is more different than another, but a 6 is not necessarily twice a 3. And sometimes no map reproduces the distances themselves, but one reproduces their order. Non-metric MDS (Shepard 1962, Kruskal 1964) uses only the order. It looks for points whose distances come in the same order as the table, as far as possible. The fit is measured by the stress, \[ \text{stress}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{s<t}\big(d^{\,\text{map}}_{st}-\hat d_{st}\big)^2}{\sum_{s<t}\big(d^{\,\text{map}}_{st}\big)^2}} , \] where \(d^{\,\text{map}}_{st}\) are the distances on the map and \(\hat d_{st}\) the numbers closest to them that come in the order of the table, fitted to the map distances. Kruskal’s rule of thumb: 20% or more is poor, 10% fair, 5% or less good, 0 perfect. The loop road shows what this buys. Classical MDS cannot reproduce its travel times without waiting: they have negative eigenvalues (Section 5.6), and the two-dimensional map stretches every distance (Section 5.7). But the order of the travel times is exactly the order of straight-line distances between points on a circle: the longer the trip around the loop, the further apart two points are across the circle, up to half a turn. So non-metric MDS fits the order perfectly, with a stress of zero: fig_nonmetric <- function() { Y <- loop_iso$points d <- tibble(place = places$place, x = Y[, 1], y = Y[, 2]) p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + axes0 + geom_path(data = bind_rows(d, d[1, ]), colour = "#cccccc", linewidth = 2.5) + geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#2c3e50") + geom_text_repel(aes(label = place), size = 3.8, seed = 3, colour = "#2c3e50") + coord_equal() + labs(title = "Non-metric MDS of the travel times", subtitle = sprintf("no waiting; stress %.1f%%; grey line: the road", loop_iso$stress), x = "dimension 1", y = "dimension 2") sh <- tibble(x = loop_shep$x, y = loop_shep$y, yf = loop_shep$yf) p2 <- ggplot(sh, aes(x, y)) + geom_step(aes(y = yf), colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#2c3e50") + labs(title = "Shepard diagram", subtitle = "red: the best order-preserving fit", x = "travel time in the table (minutes)", y = "distance on the map") p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1)) } # draw the figure fig_nonmetric() The map is a ring with the places in driving order. In the Shepard diagram every pair of places sits on the red steps: a longer trip always means a longer distance on the map. In R: library(MASS) loop_iso <- isoMDS(as.dist(D_wait(0)), k = 2) # non-metric MDS in two dimensions loop_iso$stress # in percent Check your understanding Non-metric MDS is useful when only the order of the distances can be trusted the distances are Euclidean there are more variables than observations the map has to be upside down A stress of 4% means that the map is a poor fit is a good fit has four dimensions has four negative eigenvalues Answers 1 a. 2 b. 5.9 Summary MDS starts from a distance matrix \(\mathbf D\) and finds coordinates whose straight-line distances reproduce it. The travel times of the loop road give a ring, and with a long wait at the construction site a line. \(\mathbf D\) determines the points only up to a shift, a rotation and a reflection: the states come back in the right shape, but possibly upside down. Classical MDS turns squared distances into inner products by double centring, \(\mathbf B=-\tfrac12\mathbf J\mathbf D^{(2)}\mathbf J\), and takes the coordinates from the eigendecomposition \(\mathbf B=\mathbf VK \mathbf V'\), as \(\mathbf VK^{1/2}\). For Euclidean distances it returns the principal component scores. So it goes from distances straight to latent coordinates, without choosing the orientation of a map first. A first step that turns the map into place is needed only when the latent coordinates must know which axis is which variable, as with Cholesky. In AI, embeddings are coordinates whose geometry reproduces how words are used: words that appear near each other in text end up close. Before any learning, one-hot encoding turns each token into a unit vector, with all words equally far apart. Many distances are not Euclidean (Manhattan, great circle, travel times, distances in a text). The sign is negative eigenvalues of \(\mathbf B\), which no number of extra dimensions removes. The share of the eigenvalues and the Shepard diagram show how good the map is. Non-metric MDS uses only the order of the distances and measures the fit by the stress. 5.9.1 Further reading Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 4: classical MDS with the airline distances between ten US cities, the Egyptian skulls and the water voles; non-metric MDS with voting in the House of Representatives and judgements of World War II leaders; and correspondence analysis. Borg and Groenen (2005), Modern Multidimensional Scaling: the standard reference. Schoenberg (1935) and Young and Householder (1938) on when a table of distances fits a set of points; Gower (1966) on principal coordinates; Kruskal (1964) on non-metric MDS and the stress; Mardia, Kent and Bibby (1979), Multivariate Analysis, Chapter 14, on the fit criteria. Mikolov et al. (2013) on word2vec, and Levy and Goldberg (2014), “Neural word embedding as implicit matrix factorization”, on why learned embeddings and factorising a table of word pairs are close relatives. Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing, the chapter on vector semantics and embeddings. 3Blue1Brown, But what is a GPT?, for tokens, embeddings and directions that carry meaning.
