6 Exploratory Factor Analysis R code for this chapter: efa_figures.R (data and figures) and _common.R (shared helpers). Save both in one folder and run source("efa_figures.R"); every figure is then one function call, as shown under the Code buttons. Slides for this chapter: efa_slides.html (opens in a new tab; use the arrow keys to move between slides). Variables often move together because a few hidden forces drive them all. A factor model describes exactly that: a few common factors move all the variables, and each variable also has a unique shock of its own. The Introduction met the idea with two food critics (Section 1.7.1), and this chapter starts from the same example. PCA (Chapter 4) explains the variances of the variables, with as many shocks as variables. A factor model explains the covariances between the variables: only the common factors move several variables at once, so only they create covariance. With two critics, though, the data cannot tell how much of each rating comes from the common factor and how much from the critic’s own quirks. This chapter shows that a third critic settles the question and that a fourth makes the model testable. With two or more factors an old problem returns: the factors can be turned without changing the fit, as in PCA and MDS, and the conventions for choosing the turn are called rotations. The chapter then estimates the factors behind each observation (factor scores), analyses the state indicators of Chapter 2, and compares factor analysis with PCA. The analysis is exploratory: the number of factors, and which variables depend on which factor, are left for the data to suggest. In confirmatory factor analysis (Chapter 8) they are fixed in advance, from theory. 6.1 Two critics, one quality 6.1.1 Why two ratings move together Two food critics rate the same restaurants. Their ratings are correlated: a restaurant that one critic likes, the other tends to like as well. The reason is that both taste the same food. The restaurant’s quality is a common factor, a hidden force that moves both ratings. Each critic also has her own quirks and her good and bad evenings, a unique shock that moves only her own rating. Measure each rating as a deviation from the critic’s average rating, and write \(f_t\) for the quality of restaurant \(t\). The two ratings are then \[ \begin{aligned} x_{t1}&=\lambda_1f_t+u_{t1},\\ x_{t2}&=\lambda_2f_t+u_{t2}. \end{aligned} \] The quality \(f_t\) has mean zero and variance one, so it has no units: \(f_t=1\) means a restaurant one standard deviation better than average. The loading \(\lambda_i\) (lambda) says by how many points critic \(i\)’s rating rises when the quality rises by one standard deviation. The unique shock \(u_{ti}\) holds critic \(i\)’s quirks. Its variance \(\psi_i\) (psi) is her unique variance. The quirks are uncorrelated with the quality and with each other. The figure shows the ratings of many restaurants. The purple arrow, \((\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\), is what one standard deviation of quality does to the two ratings. The blue and red arrows, of lengths \(\sqrt{\psi_1}\) and \(\sqrt{\psi_2}\), are one standard deviation of each critic’s quirks. Each quirk moves only one rating, so its arrow lies along one axis. fig_factor_choices(nrow = 1, pick = 3, critics = TRUE, panels = c("", "", "", "")) + labs(title = "Two critics, one restaurant quality", subtitle = "purple λ: quality · blue, red: each critic's quirks") 6.1.2 Only quality creates covariance The quality and the two quirks are uncorrelated, so the variances and the covariance of the ratings follow from the rule for linear combinations (Section 3.5.4): \[ \operatorname{Var}(x_{t1})=\lambda_1^2+\psi_1,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(x_{t2})=\lambda_2^2+\psi_2,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(x_{t1},x_{t2})=\lambda_1\lambda_2 . \] Each variance has a common part, \(\lambda_i^2\), and a unique part, \(\psi_i\). The covariance has only a common part. The quirks add to the variances, but they never make the two ratings move together. Only the quality does. 6.1.3 More shocks than ratings The quality and the two quirks are three shocks, but there are only two ratings. Write each quirk as its standard deviation times a shock with variance one, \(u_{ti}=\sqrt{\psi_i}\,\varepsilon_{ti}\). The model then has the form \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) of the Introduction, \[ \begin{pmatrix}x_{t1}\\ x_{t2}\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1&\sqrt{\psi_1}&0\\ \lambda_2&0&\sqrt{\psi_2}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}f_t\\ \varepsilon_{t1}\\ \varepsilon_{t2}\end{pmatrix} , \] but now \(A\) has more columns than rows. Its two zeros say that each critic’s quirks move only her own rating. 6.1.4 The data leave one number open The covariance matrix of the two ratings holds three numbers: two variances and one covariance. The model has four parameters, \(\lambda_1\), \(\lambda_2\), \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\). So the data fix three of them, and one is left open: how the noise is split between the two critics. 3 numbers in the covariance matrix, 4 parameters: one number is left open. Two numbers help to read the stories. Variable \(i\) responds to each factor with its own loading: \[ x_{ti}=\lambda_{i1}f_{t1}+\lambda_{i2}f_{t2}+\dots+\lambda_{ik}f_{tk}+u_{ti},\qquad i=1,\dots,p . \] The loading \(\lambda_{il}\) says by how much variable \(i\) moves when factor \(l\) rises by one standard deviation. The factors are uncorrelated and have variance one. The unique shocks are uncorrelated with each other and with the factors, and \(\psi_i\) is the variance of \(u_{ti}\). Stacking the \(p\) equations gives the matrix form, the factor model \[ \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}x_{t1}\\ \vdots\\ x_{tp}\end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf x_t} =\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{11}&\cdots&\lambda_{1k}\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ \lambda_{p1}&\cdots&\lambda_{pk}\end{pmatrix}}_{\Lambda} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}f_{t1}\\ \vdots\\ f_{tk}\end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf f_t} +\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}u_{t1}\\ \vdots\\ u_{tp}\end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf u_t}, \qquad\text{in short}\qquad \mathbf x_t=\Lambda\,\mathbf f_t+\mathbf u_t , \] with three parts: \(\mathbf f_t\) holds the \(k\) common factors, with \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf f_t)=I\). \(\Lambda\) (capital lambda) is the \(p\times k\) matrix of loadings. \(\mathbf u_t\) holds the \(p\) unique shocks, and \(\Psi\) (capital psi) is the diagonal matrix with the unique variances \(\psi_1,\dots,\psi_p\) on its diagonal. For the four critics, \(k=1\): \(\Lambda\) is the single column \((\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4)'\), and \(\mathbf f_t\) is the single number \(f_t\). (The factors \(\mathbf f_t=\Delta\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) of Chapter 4 had units. Here, as in most books on factor analysis, the factors have variance one, so their units sit in the loadings.) 6.2.3 The covariances The variances and covariances follow as for the two critics. With \(\sigma_{ij}\) the covariance of variables \(i\) and \(j\) and \(\sigma_{ii}\) the variance of variable \(i\), \[ \sigma_{ii}=\sum_{l=1}^k\lambda_{il}^2+\psi_i ,\qquad\qquad \sigma_{ij}=\sum_{l=1}^k\lambda_{il}\lambda_{jl}\quad(i\neq j). \] The covariances come from the common factors alone. Each variance splits into a common part \(\sum_l\lambda_{il}^2\) and a unique part \(\psi_i\). The share of the common part, \(h_i=\sum_l\lambda_{il}^2/\sigma_{ii}\), is the variable’s communality, as for the two critics. For standardised variables, with variance one, the communality is the common part itself, \(h_i=\sum_l\lambda_{il}^2\), and \(\psi_i=1-h_i\) is called the uniqueness. (Many books write the communality as \(h_i^2\).) In matrix form, all these equations together read (Section 3.5.4) \[ \Sigma=\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda\mathbf f_t)+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf u_t)=\Lambda\,I\,\Lambda'+\Psi =\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi . \] 6.2.4 More shocks than variables In the language of the Introduction, the factor model is a structural form with more shocks than variables. Divide each unique shock by its standard deviation, and stack the factors and these shocks into one vector \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) of \(k+p\) uncorrelated shocks with variance one: \[ \mathbf x_t=\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda & \Psi^{1/2}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf f_t\\ \Psi^{-1/2}\mathbf u_t\end{pmatrix}=A\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t , \] where \(\Psi^{1/2}\) is the diagonal matrix of the standard deviations \(\sqrt{\psi_i}\). The matrix \(A\) has \(p\) rows and \(k+p\) columns. For the two critics it is the matrix of Section 6.1. The factor model is the restriction that the last \(p\) columns of \(A\) form a diagonal matrix: each unique shock moves only its own variable. Estimation software stops at the boundary and reports a unique variance of almost zero: factanal() does not let a uniqueness fall below 0.005, so a reported 0.005 signals a Heywood case. Section 6.8 meets such a case. Why does it happen here? With one factor, each covariance is the product of two loadings. Critics 2 and 3 now barely agree, so quality must play only a small part in their ratings. For critic 1 to agree as closely as she does with both of them, quality would then have to explain more than all of her rating variance. A second factor removes the contradiction. So the six covariances are built from just four numbers. Pair up the four critics in the three possible ways and multiply: \[ \sigma_{12}\sigma_{34}=\sigma_{13}\sigma_{24}=\sigma_{14}\sigma_{23}=\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3\lambda_4 . \] Here \(0.75\times0.54=0.45\times0.90 =0.675\times0.60=0.405\). These two equalities are the restrictions, Spearman’s tetrad conditions. A covariance matrix that violates them cannot come from one factor. A tetrad is a group of four: each condition ties together the covariances of four variables, and with more variables every group of four must satisfy them. Two or more factors restrict \(\Sigma\) in other ways, and the likelihood ratio test of Section 6.5 checks all the restrictions at once, whatever their form. 6.4.2 Counting restrictions The same count works for any number of variables \(p\) and factors \(k\). \(\Sigma\) holds \(p(p+1)/2\) numbers: \(p\) variances and \(p(p-1)/2\) covariances. The model has \(pk\) loadings and \(p\) unique variances. With two or more factors, though, the factors can be turned without changing \(\Sigma\) (Section 6.6). A turn of \(k\) factors has \(k(k-1)/2\) angles, which the data cannot fix, so they do not count as unknowns. The difference is the number of restrictions, the degrees of freedom of the model: \[ \text{df}=\frac{p(p+1)}{2}-\Big(pk+p-\frac{k(k-1)}{2}\Big)=\frac{(p-k)^2-(p+k)}{2} . \] (Multiply out both sides to check.) For two critics, \(\text{df}=-1\): one number short, the free parameter. For three, \(\text{df}=0\): just identified. For four, \(\text{df}=2\): the two tetrad conditions. A positive count means that the model can be tested with data: efa_df <- function(p, k) ((p - k)^2 - (p + k)) / 2 fig_efa_count <- function(pmax = 10, kmax = 4) { d <- expand_grid(p = 2:pmax, k = 1:kmax) |> filter(k < p) |> mutate(df = efa_df(p, k), status = factor(case_when(df < 0 ~ "not identified", df == 0 ~ "just identified", TRUE ~ "testable"), levels = c("not identified", "just identified", "testable"))) ggplot(d, aes(p, k, fill = status)) + geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) + geom_text(aes(label = df), size = 4.2, colour = "#2c3e50") + scale_fill_manual(values = c(`not identified` = "#f4c7c3", `just identified` = "#fde9b8", testable = "#cfe8d4"), name = NULL) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:pmax, expand = c(0, 0)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:kmax, expand = c(0, 0)) + coord_equal() + labs(x = "number of variables p", y = "number of factors k", subtitle = "number in each tile: covariances left over after fitting the model (degrees of freedom)") + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "top", plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11)) } # draw the figure fig_efa_count() Factors use up covariances fast. With the six state indicators, three factors would leave nothing to test. A non-negative count is needed, but it is not always enough. With data, the sample covariance matrix \(S\) takes its place, and sampling noise breaks the tetrad conditions a little, so that no \(\lambda\lambda'+\Psi\) reproduces \(S\) exactly. Estimation finds the loadings and unique variances whose \(\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi\) comes closest to \(S\). The test asks whether the remaining gap is larger than sampling noise would produce. To see how this works, let the four critics rate 200 restaurants, simulated from the path diagram above, so that we know the truth. R’s factanal() does both steps: crit_fa <- factanal(crit_X, factors = 1) # crit_X: 200 restaurants rated by the four critics crit_fa ## ## Call: ## factanal(x = crit_X, factors = 1) ## ## Uniquenesses: ## critic 1 critic 2 critic 3 critic 4 ## 0.517 0.160 0.685 0.188 ## ## Loadings: ## Factor1 ## critic 1 0.695 ## critic 2 0.917 ## critic 3 0.561 ## critic 4 0.901 ## ## Factor1 ## SS loadings 2.451 ## Proportion Var 0.613 ## ## Test of the hypothesis that 1 factor is sufficient. ## The chi square statistic is 1.26 on 2 degrees of freedom. ## The p-value is 0.533 factanal() works with standardised ratings, so it reports the loadings \(\lambda_i/\sqrt{\sigma_{ii}}\) and the uniquenesses \(\psi_i/\sigma_{ii}\). The true values are 0.75, 0.89, 0.60 and 0.90 for the loadings and 0.44, 0.20, 0.64 and 0.19 for the uniquenesses, and the estimates from 200 restaurants are close. “SS loadings” is the sum of the squared loadings, the common variance of the four critics together, and “Proportion Var” its share of the total variance, four. 6.5.2 Maximum likelihood factanal() estimates by maximum likelihood. It assumes that the observations are normal (Section 3.4) and picks the \(\Lambda\) and \(\Psi\) under which the observed sample is most probable. This turns out to be the same as making the discrepancy \[ F_{\text{ML}}(\Lambda,\Psi)=\ln|\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi|+\operatorname{tr}\!\big(S(\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi)^{-1}\big)-\ln|S|-p \] as small as possible, where \(|\cdot|\) is the determinant and \(\operatorname{tr}\) the trace (Section 4.2). \(F_{\text{ML}}\) is zero when \(\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi=S\) and positive otherwise, so it measures how far the covariance matrix of the model is from that of the sample. There is no formula for the minimum: factanal() searches for it numerically. Where the discrepancy FML comes from Here \(\mathbf x_t\) stands for an observation as measured, not yet centred. Its normal density is \((2\pi)^{-p/2}|\Sigma|^{-1/2}\exp\!\big(-\tfrac12(\mathbf x_t-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x_t-\mu)\big)\) (Section 3.4). The observations are independent, so the density of the whole sample is the product of these over \(t=1,\dots,n\). Read as a function of the parameters, it is the likelihood \(L\), and its logarithm is \[ \ln L=-\frac{np}{2}\ln(2\pi)-\frac n2\ln|\Sigma|-\frac12\sum_{t=1}^n(\mathbf x_t-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x_t-\mu) . \] Whatever \(\Sigma\) is, the sum is smallest, and \(L\) largest, at \(\mu=\bar{\mathbf x}\), the sample mean, so we can set \(\mu=\bar{\mathbf x}\). Each term of the sum is a single number, so it equals its own trace, and a trace does not change when the factors of a product are cycled: \((\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})'\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})=\operatorname{tr}\big(\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})(\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})'\big)\). Summing over \(t\) and using \(\sum_t(\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})(\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})'=(n-1)S\) turns the sum into \((n-1)\operatorname{tr}(S\Sigma^{-1})\), and with \(n-1\approx n\), \[ \ln L\approx\text{constant}-\frac n2\Big(\ln|\Sigma|+\operatorname{tr}(S\Sigma^{-1})\Big). \] So the likelihood is largest where \(\ln|\Sigma|+\operatorname{tr}(S\Sigma^{-1})\) is smallest. Without any restriction on \(\Sigma\), the smallest value, \(\ln|S|+p\), is reached at \(\Sigma=S\). Subtracting it gives \(F_{\text{ML}}\), which is therefore never negative. 6.5.3 Testing the restrictions If the model is right, the minimum of \(F_{\text{ML}}\) is small: only sampling noise keeps the covariance matrix of the model from matching \(S\). The likelihood ratio test turns this into a test. Its statistic is the minimum of \(F_{\text{ML}}\) times about \(n\) (precisely \(n-1-(2p+5)/6-2k/3\), a small-sample correction). If the model is right, the statistic has approximately a chi-square distribution (Section 3.4.4) with df degrees of freedom, and as for Alaska in Section 3.6.5, a value far out in its tail is surprising. The p-value is the probability, if the model is right, of a statistic at least as large as the one observed. A small p-value says that the gap between the model and the data is larger than sampling noise usually produces. For the four critics, the statistic is 1.26 on 2 degrees of freedom, with a p-value of 0.533: no evidence against one factor. Now change the story. Critics 3 and 4 dine together: they visit each restaurant on the same evening and share their bad evenings, so their quirks are correlated (0.5 in the simulation). Their ratings then have more in common than quality, and one factor no longer describes the four critics: crit_fa2 <- factanal(crit_X2, factors = 1) # crit_X2: critics 3 and 4 dine together unname(crit_fa2$STATISTIC) # the chi-square statistic, on 2 degrees of freedom ## [1] 20.41691 unname(crit_fa2$PVAL) # its p-value ## [1] 3.685743e-05 The statistic jumps to 20.4, with a p-value below 0.0001, and one factor is rejected. The tetrads show where the misfit sits: f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3) crit_tetrads <- function(X) { S <- cov(X); c(S[1, 2] * S[3, 4], S[1, 3] * S[2, 4], S[1, 4] * S[2, 3]) } f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3) ptxt <- function(p) if (p < 1e-4) "< 0.0001" else if (p < 0.001) paste("=", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 4)) else paste("=", f3(p)) fig_crit_tetrads <- function() { lab <- c("s₁₂ · s₃₄", "s₁₃ · s₂₄", "s₁₄ · s₂₃") d <- bind_rows( tibble(sample = sprintf("One quality factor\ntest of one factor: p-value %s", ptxt(crit_fa$PVAL)), prod = lab, v = crit_tetrads(crit_X)), tibble(sample = sprintf("Critics 3 and 4 dine together\ntest of one factor: p-value %s", ptxt(crit_fa2$PVAL)), prod = lab, v = crit_tetrads(crit_X2))) |> mutate(sample = factor(sample, levels = unique(sample)), prod = factor(prod, levels = lab)) ggplot(d, aes(prod, v)) + geom_col(fill = col_f, width = 0.6) + geom_text(aes(label = f3(v)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) + facet_wrap(~ sample) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.55), expand = c(0, 0)) + labs(x = NULL, y = "product of two sample covariances") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11.5, face = "bold"), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12)) } # draw the figure fig_crit_tetrads() With one quality factor, the three products of sample covariances agree, up to sampling noise. (All three also lie a little below the value 0.405 of the model, by chance; the test asks only whether they agree with each other.) When critics 3 and 4 dine together, their covariance \(s_{34}\) contains their shared evenings as well as quality, and the product \(s_{12}s_{34}\) sticks out. The test only says that the model does not fit. The tetrads say a little more: one of the two pairs, critics 1 and 2 or critics 3 and 4, shares more than quality. Which pair it is, the data cannot tell; here we know it from the story. A test that does not reject is no proof either: with fewer restaurants, the shared evenings might have gone unnoticed. 6.5.4 The units do not matter Suppose critic 1 rated on a 100-point scale instead of a 10-point one, so that all her ratings were ten times larger. Multiplying her equation by ten gives \[ 10\,x_{t1}=(10\lambda_1)\,f_t+10\,u_{t1}=(10\lambda_1)\,f_t+\big(10\sqrt{\psi_1}\big)\,\varepsilon_{t1} . \] Everything measured in rating points is ten times as large: her loading, her quirk \(u_{t1}\) and its standard deviation \(\sqrt{\psi_1}\), so her unique variance is a hundred times as large. The shocks measured in standard deviations do not change at all: the quality \(f_t\) and her standardised quirk \(\varepsilon_{t1}=u_{t1}/\sqrt{\psi_1}\) are the same numbers as before, restaurant by restaurant. Only her unique shock in rating points changes: \(10u_{t1}\) is perfectly correlated with the old \(u_{t1}\), but ten times as large. In general, a change of units multiplies each variable by a positive number, \(x_{ti}\) by \(\alpha_i\), here with \(\alpha=(10,1,1,1)\). With \(\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\) the diagonal matrix with \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_p\) on its diagonal, the structural form of Section 6.2 becomes \[ \operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\,\mathbf x_t=\big(\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\,A\big)\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t =\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\Lambda & \operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\Psi^{1/2}\end{pmatrix} \boldsymbol\varepsilon_t . \] The change of units multiplies row \(i\) of \(A\) by \(\alpha_i\) and leaves the shocks \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\), the factors and the standardised unique shocks, exactly as they were. The new \(A\) still has a diagonal block, so the rescaled variables follow a factor model driven by the same shocks, with loadings \(\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\Lambda\) and unique variances \(\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\,\Psi\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\). The estimates rescale in the same way. The covariance matrix of the rescaled ratings is \(\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\,S\,\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\), and each candidate \(\Sigma=\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi\) for the original ratings corresponds to the candidate \(\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\,\Sigma\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\) for the rescaled ones. The two fit equally well. The discrepancy depends on the two matrices only through \(\Sigma^{-1}S\), since \(F_{\text{ML}}=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}S)-\ln|\Sigma^{-1}S|-p\), and the rescaling turns \(\Sigma^{-1}S\) into \(\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)^{-1}\,\Sigma^{-1}S\,\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)\), which has the same trace and the same determinant. So the best fit to the rescaled ratings is the rescaled best fit. Here is the check, with the fit of factanal() written in the critics’ own units: F_ml <- function(S, Sigma) { SiS <- solve(Sigma, S); sum(diag(SiS)) - log(det(SiS)) - nrow(S) } S <- cov(crit_X); sdv <- sqrt(diag(S)) lam <- crit_fa$loadings[, 1] * sdv # the estimated loadings, in the critics' own units psi <- crit_fa$uniquenesses * sdv^2 # the estimated unique variances, in the same units alpha <- c(10, 1, 1, 1) # critic 1 on a ten times wider scale c(original = F_ml(S, lam %o% lam + diag(psi)), rescaled = F_ml(diag(alpha) %*% S %*% diag(alpha), (alpha * lam) %o% (alpha * lam) + diag(alpha^2 * psi))) ## original rescaled ## 0.006407872 0.006407872 Both discrepancies are 0.00641. Multiplied by \(n-1-(2p+5)/6-2k/3=196.2\), this is the test statistic 1.26 of the four critics. So factor analysis by maximum likelihood is scale-invariant. A change of units multiplies the estimated loadings of variable \(i\) by \(\alpha_i\) and its estimated unique variance by \(\alpha_i^2\), as in the model, and leaves everything without units unchanged: the fit, the test, the loadings and uniquenesses of the standardised variables that factanal() reports, and the estimated factors (Section 6.7). That is why the covariance matrix and the correlation matrix give the same answer, and why factanal() can standardise the variables before it fits, and work with the correlation matrix, without losing anything. PCA is not scale-invariant. It looks for the directions of largest variance, and a change of units changes them (Section 4.5), so the components themselves change, not just their units. With critic 1 on the 100-point scale, her rating has most of the variance, and the first principal component is almost her rating alone: pc_old <- prcomp(crit_X) # PCA of the original ratings pc_new <- prcomp(crit_X %*% diag(alpha)) # critic 1 on the 100-point scale # abs(): the sign of a component is arbitrary round(abs(pc_new$rotation[, 1]), 2) # the weights of the new first component ## [1] 0.99 0.07 0.04 0.06 abs(cor(pc_old$x[, 1], pc_new$x[, 1])) # its correlation with the old first component ## [1] 0.8086944 The new first component has a correlation of only 0.81 with the old one. It is a different variable, not the old component in new units. Factor analysis splits each variance into a common and a unique part. Rescaling a variable multiplies both parts by the same number, so the shares do not move, and neither do the factor, the fit or the test. PCA looks for the largest variance, and a variable whose numbers are ten times larger has a hundred times the variance, so it takes over the first component. That is why PCA is usually applied to the correlation matrix, as for the states (Section 6.8), while factor analysis gives the same answer either way. A school gives 200 students six tests, three verbal tests (reading, vocabulary and grammar) and three mathematics tests (arithmetic, algebra and geometry). The six test scores are the observed variables, so \(p=6\). Behind them are two abilities, the students’ verbal ability and their mathematical ability. Nobody observes an ability directly: the abilities are latent, or unobserved, variables, the \(k=2\) common factors of the model, just as the quality of a restaurant was seen only through the critics’ ratings. We want to estimate the abilities from the six observed scores. Keep in mind what the analysis below is told: the scores and the number of factors, but not which test is which. The factor model of this chapter has uncorrelated factors, and the correlated factors of the diagram fit into it. With a correlation matrix \(\Phi\) for the factors, the covariance matrix is \(\Sigma=\Lambda\Phi\Lambda'+\Psi\), and \(\Lambda\Phi\Lambda'=(\Lambda\Phi^{1/2})(\Lambda\Phi^{1/2})'\), with \(\Phi^{1/2}\) the symmetric root of \(\Phi\). So the same \(\Sigma\) also comes from uncorrelated factors, with loadings \(\Lambda\Phi^{1/2}\). In these loadings every test loads on both factors, although in the diagram it depends on one ability only. Reading, for example, has the loading 0.8 on verbal ability, and with uncorrelated factors the loadings \(0.8\times(0.97, 0.26)=(0.77, 0.21)\). So the estimates below show small loadings on the other factor as well. The analysis starts with uncorrelated factors, and Section 6.6.5 brings the correlation back. Do the data reveal two factors? This is the usual way to choose the number of factors: start with one, and add factors until the test no longer rejects or no degrees of freedom are left (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 5.6). With many observations the test finds even small, unimportant gaps, so how readable the factors are counts as well. 6.6.2 Every turn fits the data With two factors, each test has two loadings, \((\lambda_{i1},\lambda_{i2})\), a point in the plane. Their distances from the origin stay the same, and so do the angles between them. The squared distance of test \(i\) from the origin is its communality, \(h_i=\lambda_{i1}^2+\lambda_{i2}^2\), and the inner product of two points is the correlation of the two tests, \(\sigma_{ij}=\lambda_{i1}\lambda_{j1}+\lambda_{i2}\lambda_{j2}\). So no correlation and no communality changes, and every turn fits the data equally well. This is the rotation problem of the Introduction, now confined to the common factors. The unique shocks cannot be turned, because each must keep moving only its own variable. Two factors can be turned by one angle. Three factors need three angles (roll, pitch and yaw, Section 5.2), and \(k\) factors need \(k(k-1)/2\). These are the angles subtracted in the count of Section 6.4. The computer still has to report one turn. factanal() chooses it much as PCA would: the first factor carries as much of the common variance as it can, and the second as much of the rest (after each variable is divided by the standard deviation of its unique shock). That is the frame “as estimated”. The first factor loads on all six tests, a general factor, and the second is a contrast, negative for the verbal tests and positive for the mathematics tests. It describes the correlations correctly, but it hides the two abilities. 6.6.3 Simple structure and varimax Which turn should we report? Thurstone’s (1947) answer is simple structure: each variable should load mainly on one factor, so that each factor can be read off from a few variables. Kaiser’s (1958) varimax criterion makes this precise. For each factor, take the squared loadings of the \(p\) variables and compute their variance across the variables. This variance is large when the squared loadings are either near zero or large, and small when they are all middling. Varimax turns the factors until the sum of these variances, the varimax criterion \[ \sum_{l=1}^k\Bigg[\frac1p\sum_{i=1}^p\Big(\frac{\lambda_{il}}{\sqrt{h_i}}\Big)^4-\bigg(\frac1p\sum_{i=1}^p\Big(\frac{\lambda_{il}}{\sqrt{h_i}}\Big)^2\bigg)^2\Bigg], \] is as large as possible. Dividing each loading by \(\sqrt{h_i}\), the square root of the variable’s communality, makes every variable count equally (Kaiser’s normalisation, the default in R). The slider of Section 6.6.2 shows the criterion above the plot, for every turn. As estimated, it is 0.055. The button “varimax” turns the factors by \(-34^\circ\), where the criterion reaches its maximum, 0.363: the verbal tests then lie close to one axis and the mathematics tests close to the other. (A turn of \(56^\circ\) gives the same maximum. It is the same solution, with the two factors swapped and one of them reversed in sign.) After the varimax turn, the verbal tests load 0.84, 0.64 and 0.55 on the first factor and the mathematics tests 0.74, 0.63 and 0.53 on the second, and the cross-loadings are small, between 0.12 and 0.28. The first factor is verbal ability, the second mathematical ability: tests_fv <- factanal(tests_X, factors = 2) # varimax is the default rotation print(tests_fv$loadings, cutoff = 0) ## ## Loadings: ## Factor1 Factor2 ## reading 0.842 0.206 ## vocabulary 0.638 0.172 ## grammar 0.552 0.194 ## arithmetic 0.278 0.744 ## algebra 0.137 0.635 ## geometry 0.122 0.532 ## ## Factor1 Factor2 ## SS loadings 1.532 1.349 ## Proportion Var 0.255 0.225 ## Cumulative Var 0.255 0.480 6.6.4 The data find the groups, we name them factanal() was never told which test is which. It found the two groups from the correlations alone: the three verbal tests are more correlated with each other than with the mathematics tests, and the same holds for the mathematics tests. So the points of the verbal tests lie close together in the plane of loadings, and so do those of the mathematics tests, and varimax turns the axes until each passes through one group. What the data cannot supply is the names. That the first factor is verbal ability we know only because the tests that load on it are reading, vocabulary and grammar. The states in Section 6.8 work the same way: varimax finds groups of indicators, and the names come from what the indicators measure. Confirmatory factor analysis (Chapter 8) goes the other way round. There the analyst says in advance which variable loads on which factor, by setting the other loadings to zero, and the data only estimate the rest. Those zeros also remove the freedom to turn the factors. 6.6.5 Correlated factors: promax Varimax keeps the factors uncorrelated: their axes stay at right angles. But the two abilities go together, and no pair of perpendicular axes can pass through both groups of tests. An oblique rotation lets the factors correlate. The model becomes \(\mathbf x_t=\Lambda\mathbf f_t+\mathbf u_t\) with \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf f_t)=\Phi\), the correlation matrix of the factors, so that \(\Sigma=\Lambda\Phi\Lambda'+\Psi\). Promax puts the two axes 60° apart, which corresponds to a factor correlation of \(\cos 60^\circ=0.50\), the value used in the simulation. The promax loadings of a test are its coordinates along the tilted axes, each read off parallel to the other axis. Its cross-loading then almost vanishes, between -0.06 and 0.07. The main loadings are 0.87, 0.65 and 0.55 for the verbal tests and 0.76, 0.68 and 0.56 for the mathematics tests, close to the true 0.8, 0.7 and 0.6: tests_fp <- factanal(tests_X, factors = 2, rotation = "promax") tests_fp # loadings, factor correlations and the test ## ## Call: ## factanal(x = tests_X, factors = 2, rotation = "promax") ## ## Uniquenesses: ## reading vocabulary grammar arithmetic algebra geometry ## 0.249 0.563 0.658 0.369 0.579 0.702 ## ## Loadings: ## Factor1 Factor2 ## reading 0.867 ## vocabulary 0.652 ## grammar 0.549 ## arithmetic 0.761 ## algebra 0.676 ## geometry 0.565 ## ## Factor1 Factor2 ## SS loadings 1.487 1.360 ## Proportion Var 0.248 0.227 ## Cumulative Var 0.248 0.474 ## ## Factor Correlations: ## Factor1 Factor2 ## Factor1 1.000 0.504 ## Factor2 0.504 1.000 ## ## Test of the hypothesis that 2 factors are sufficient. ## The chi square statistic is 1.59 on 4 degrees of freedom. ## The p-value is 0.811 With correlated factors, the loadings are still the weights in \(\mathbf x_t=\Lambda\mathbf f_t+\mathbf u_t\), the pattern. They are no longer the correlations between the variables and the factors, the structure \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf f_t)=\Lambda\Phi\), because each variable is also correlated with a factor through the other factor. In the figure, the structure is what a perpendicular projection onto each tilted axis would read off. And the common variance of test \(i\) is now the \(i\)-th diagonal entry of \(\Lambda\Phi\Lambda'\), no longer the sum of its squared loadings. So the “SS loadings” and “Proportion Var” that factanal() prints for promax are not shares of the variance. Rotation changes the description, not the fit. Every turn and every tilt gives the same covariance matrix, the same communalities and the same test. Choosing a rotation is choosing how to describe the factors, just as PCA chose \(A\) for convenience (Section 4.8). The names verbal and mathematical fit here because we know what each test asks. With real data, the names are interpretations. With three or more critics, the covariance matrix pins them down (Section 6.3). The shocks are another matter: the quality of each restaurant, and the quirks behind each rating. In the earlier chapters, the parameters gave the shocks for free. There, \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) had as many shocks as variables, so \(A\) was square. Once \(A\) was chosen, it could be undone, \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t=A^{-1}\mathbf x_t\), and every shock followed exactly from the data. The PCA scores \(\mathbf f_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t\) are an example (Section 4.2). Whether a matrix can be undone depends on its shape: More rows than columns, that is, more variables than shocks. Then \(A\) can still be undone, as long as no column is a combination of the others: the matrix \((A'A)^{-1}A'\) does it, because \((A'A)^{-1}A'A=I\). If the four critics had no quirks, for example, each rating would be \(x_{ti}=\lambda_if_t\), \(A\) would be the single column \((\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_4)'\), and any one rating would reveal the quality exactly, \(f_t=x_{ti}/\lambda_i\). More columns than rows, that is, more shocks than variables. Then no matrix undoes \(A\), because different shocks produce the same data. The factor model is of the second kind. Its \(A=\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda&\Psi^{1/2}\end{pmatrix}\) has \(p\) rows and \(k+p\) columns (Section 6.2). The four critics give four ratings, but there are five shocks: the quality and the four quirks. Whatever quality a restaurant has, the quirks can make up the difference. For any value of \(f_t\), the quirks \(u_{ti}=x_{ti}-\lambda_if_t\) reproduce the four ratings exactly. Its peak is not where the four quirks average zero, for two reasons: a quirk counts more against a quality when it belongs to a critic whose quirks are usually small, and a quality far above the average restaurant is itself unlikely. In a factor model the parameters are identified, but the shocks are not: \(A\) has more columns than rows, so it has no inverse. The factors can only be estimated, and the estimates are called factor scores. 6.7.2 Estimating quality from four ratings Here is the idea for one factor and the four critics, with the loadings and unique variances of the model. It finds the centre of the bell curve. Each critic’s rating, divided by her loading, measures the quality with an error: \[x_{ti}/\lambda_i=f_t+u_{ti}/\lambda_i .\] The error has variance \(\psi_i/\lambda_i^2\), which is small for a critic with a large loading and small quirks. Average the four measurements, and give each a weight proportional to its precision \(\lambda_i^2/\psi_i\), one over its error variance. These weights make the error of the average as small as possible. With the total precision \(\tau=\sum_i\lambda_i^2/\psi_i\) (tau), the average is \[\hat f^{\,B}_t=\frac1\tau\sum_i\frac{\lambda_i^2}{\psi_i}\cdot\frac{x_{ti}}{\lambda_i}=\frac1\tau\sum_i\frac{\lambda_i}{\psi_i}\,x_{ti}.\] Its error, \(\frac1\tau\sum_i(\lambda_i/\psi_i)\,u_{ti}\), has variance \(\frac1{\tau^2}\sum_i(\lambda_i^2/\psi_i^2)\,\psi_i=1/\tau\). This is Bartlett’s score (Bartlett 1937), hence the \(B\). \(\hat f^{\,B}_t\) is quality plus an error, and quality has variance one, so \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat f^{\,B}_t)=1+1/\tau\). The regression of quality on \(\hat f^{\,B}_t\) has the slope \(\operatorname{Cov}(f_t,\hat f^{\,B}_t)/\operatorname{Var}(\hat f^{\,B}_t)=1/(1+1/\tau)=\tau/(1+\tau)\), so the best prediction of quality shrinks \(\hat f^{\,B}_t\) towards zero, the average quality: \[\hat f_t=\frac{\tau}{1+\tau}\,\hat f^{\,B}_t=\sum_i w_i\,x_{ti},\qquad w_i=\frac{\lambda_i/\psi_i}{1+\tau}.\] This is the regression score, the centre of the bell curve in the figure above. The weights of the four critics are 0.15, 0.36, 0.08 and 0.43. Critic 4 counts most (loading 0.90, quirk variance 0.19) and critic 3 least (0.60 and 0.64). With \(k\) factors the same idea gives \(\hat{\mathbf f}_t=\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x_t\), the regression of the factors on the variables: its coefficients are \(\Sigma^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf f_t)\), the matrix version of a covariance over a variance, and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf f_t)=\operatorname{Cov}(\Lambda\mathbf f_t+\mathbf u_t,\mathbf f_t)=\Lambda\). (With correlated factors, \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf f_t)=\Lambda\Phi\), and the scores become \(\hat{\mathbf f}_t=\Phi\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x_t\).) The scores do not depend on the units (Section 6.5.4). With critic 1 on the 100-point scale, her loading is ten times and her unique variance a hundred times as large. So her precision \(\lambda_1^2/\psi_1\) and the total precision \(\tau\) stay the same, and her weight \(w_1=(\lambda_1/\psi_1)/(1+\tau)\) becomes ten times smaller. That exactly offsets her ten times larger rating, and every restaurant gets the same score as before: the scores estimate the same quality \(f_t\). With \(k\) factors, \(\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\) becomes \(\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)^{-1}\), with the same effect. 6.7.3 The scores are never exact How well do the scores track the true quality? The regression score is Bartlett’s score times a number, so both have the same squared correlation with quality: \[ \rho^2=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(f_t,\hat f^{\,B}_t)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\operatorname{Var}(\hat f^{\,B}_t)} =\frac{1}{1+1/\tau}=\frac{\tau}{1+\tau} . \] With critic 1 alone, \(\rho^2=0.56\), her communality. Only the common factors create covariance. In the structural form \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) it has \(k+p\) shocks, and the unique shocks fill a diagonal block of \(A\). With one factor, two variables fix only the product of their loadings. A third variable pins the loadings down (just identified), and a fourth adds two testable restrictions, the tetrad conditions. In general the model has \(\text{df}=\tfrac12\big[(p-k)^2-(p+k)\big]\) restrictions. A negative or zero unique variance is a Heywood case: the model does not fit, or the sample is too small. Maximum likelihood finds the \(\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi\) closest to \(S\), and the likelihood ratio test asks whether the remaining gap is more than sampling noise. A change of units rescales the loadings and unique variances, and leaves the factors, the fit and the test as they were (scale invariance). With two or more factors, the factors can be turned without changing the fit. Varimax picks the turn with the simplest structure, and promax also lets the factors correlate. Rotation changes the description, not the fit. The data find the groups of variables, such as the verbal and the mathematics tests, but the names of the factors come from what we know about the variables. Here the data choose the turn, so the analysis is exploratory. Theory can instead fix loadings in advance, for example a zero where a test should not depend on an ability. That makes it confirmatory (Chapter 8). The parameters are identified, but the shocks are not: \(A\) has more columns than rows, so it has no inverse. Factor scores estimate the factors. Each variable counts in proportion to its loading over its unique variance, and the scores are never exact (factor indeterminacy). For the states, the tests reject one and two factors, and two factors give a Heywood case. A factor model is an approximation, and its factors are interpretations. PCA explains the variances and mixes the unique variances into its components. Factor analysis explains the covariances and sets the unique variances apart. A factor model explains the covariances by a few common factors, and keeps each variable’s own noise apart. 6.10.1 Further reading Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 5: Spearman’s example and the Heywood case, scale invariance, principal factor and maximum likelihood estimation, the test for the number of factors, rotation, factor scores, two examples (life expectancies, and drug use by American college students), and the comparison with PCA. Change in Notation Some symbols in Chapters 1 to 5 have changed, so that every symbol now has one meaning throughout the notes. The ideas, the examples and the results are the same. This page lists the changes chapter by chapter. The figures and sliders use the new symbols as well. Conventions Indices. Observations are numbered \(s\) and \(t\), variables \(i\) and \(j\), and factors, components and dimensions \(l\). The number of components or dimensions that are kept is \(k\). Bold. Bold lower-case letters are observations, such as \(\mathbf x_t\), \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) and \(\mathbf f_t\). Bold capitals are matrices with one row for each observation: the data matrix \(\mathbf X\), and in Chapter 5 also \(\mathbf D\), \(\mathbf B\), \(\mathbf J\), \(\mathbf V\) and \(\mathbf F\). Rotations. A rotation matrix is \(Q=Q(\theta)\), turning by the angle \(\theta\) (theta). A turned matrix or shock gets a tilde, as in \(\tilde A=AQ\) and \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}=Q'\boldsymbol\varepsilon\). Eigenvalues. An eigenvalue is \(\kappa\) (kappa), as in \(Sv=\kappa v\). The letter \(\lambda\) is kept for the loadings of a factor model. Splitting \(A\). \(A=C\Delta\): the diagonal matrix \(\Delta\) (capital delta) holds the standard deviations \(\delta_l\) of the factors, and \(C\) how the variables respond to one unit of each factor. In PCA, \(C\) is written \(\Gamma\).
